QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. GARDINER RESPECTING REPORTED STATEMENT OP MR. SWEEZEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to speak to a question of privilege and to refer to certain statements reflecting on my honour and integrity both as a member of the house and as a private citizen, which are contained in a newspaper, the Toronto Daily Star. I hold in my hand a copy of the Toronto Daily Star of Friday, May 23, 1930. The heading of the article is as follows:
R. O. Sweezey Assails Beauharnois Attack. Electioneering Play, Power Head Styles Demand for Probe.
Special to The Star by Staff Reporter. Ottawa, May 23. In a statement to The Star to-day, R. 0. Sweezey, president of the Beauharnois Power Corporation described the attack on Beauharnois in the house yesterday as a crude electioneering play that would deceive no honest or intelligent Canadian.
"I'm afraid," he said, "that Mr. Gardiner has been utterly deceived by a group who have
confused him with a jumble of distorted facts and deliberate falsehoods. He has shown such utter disregard for the truth that I should scarcely know where to begin in an attempt to convince him that he has been led into a silly lot of misstatements.
Intelligent investors in this country, however, know full well that last night's kind of performance in parliament is usual on the eve of a general election.
I assure all fair-minded Canadians that our undertaking is sound, honest and sincere. Ninety-nine per cent of Beauharnois Power stock is owned in Canada by Canadians, and there are several thousand shareholders.
Personally, I am very busy with engineering development work, and would as soon try to explain the Einstein theory to an Eskimo as to enter into a controversy with some people."
In the first place I want to say that Mr. Sweezey's statement, as above reported, that I have been deceived by a group who have confused me by a jumble of distorted facts and deliberate falsehoods, is utterly untrue and without foundation in fact. I have not consulted nor have I been consulted by any group, either financial or political, in reference to the Beauharnois project, and the statements made by me in the house were the result of private investigations by myself and certain of my colleagues. His statement that this attack was purely "electioneering play" on my part is not only false but deliberately misleading.
I desire to enlighten him as to both the sources of my information and the reasons which prompted my bringing this matter to the attention of the house. In doing this I am also inspired with the desire to place the facts fairly and impartially before the house and the people of the Dominion of Canada, so that they will be able to decide impartially and fairly as to whether or not what I said in the house in connection with Mr. Sweezey and the Beauharnois project was justifiable or not. In view of the statement that Mr. Sweezey made in the dispatch just quoted, namely, that he does not know where to begin in denying my statements, I propose to give him an opportunity to start by going over the main points of last Thursday's discussion in the house.
The order in council dated Friday, March 8, 1929, P.C. 422, is authority for the statement made in the house respecting the incorporation of the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company, as well as authority for the statement made in connection with the securing of the lease from the province of Quebec and the application made by the

Beauharnois Corporation-Mr. Gardiner
Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited, for approval of its plans by the Dominion government. Surely Mr. Sweezey does not hope successfully to deny the facts mentioned in this order in council, although these are the very facts that are denied by him in the newspaper despatch above indicated. Apparently his conception of the mentality of the members of the house and of the Canadian people is not very flattering, but it is quite consistent when one realizes what he has attempted to perpetrate upon an unsuspecting public. My statement that the Robert interests had to be acquired is founded upon a statement found in a letter signed by Mr. Sweezey himself and addressed to Mr. J. Alderic Raymond, brother of Senator Donat Raymond and the hon. member for Beauharnois (Mr. Raymond). I placed that letter on Hansard last Thursday and hon. members may read it there so that the time of the house may be saved. Further Mr. Sweezey has admitted under oath that he personally purchased the Robert interests referred to in this letter, which interests were essential to this undertaking. If Mr. Sweezey has forgotten about giving such evidence under oath, he can refresh his memory by reference to a transcript of the evidence given by him in connection with this matter.
The statements made in the house that the company was over-capitalized are based on statements contained in a document called " A Statement in Lieu of Prospectus," which was prepared and issued by the Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited, of which he is now president, and filed in the office of the Secretary of State, Ottawa. Mr. Speaker, I
rise to a point of order. Is an hon. member allowed to bring up a question again that has already been debated on a motion for adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance? This is not a question of privilege; it is a question of special privilege.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: QUESTION OP PRIVILEGE BY MR. GARDINER RESPECTING REPORTED STATEMENT OP MR. SWEEZEY
speechtext:
This is a question of
privilege and Bourinot says at page 303:
In the Canadian house questions of privilege take a wide range, but it may be stated in general terms that they refer to all matters affecting the nights and immunities of the house collectively, or to the position and conduct of members in their representative character. In this category may be placed: motions touching the seat or election of members; reflections or libels in books and newspapers on the house or members thereof, or any of its committees; forgery of signatures to petitions; motions for new writs; questions affecting the internal economy or proceedings of the house;
Bourinot says also that great latitude is given in the house when the question of privilege is raised. But the question of libel should be dealt with in a brief way so as not to take up the time of the house unduly. The moment the hon. gentleman has denied the statement and explained why it is not true according to his own interpretation he should not proceed much further. I understand the hon. gentleman is practically through.

Mr. Speaker, it is rather remarkable that any hon. member should question my right after I had read this statement in the press despatch:

-"that Mr. Gardiner has been utterly deceived by a group who have confused him with a jumble of distorted facts and deliberate falsehoods."
I am trying to show, Mr. Speaker, that every word I said was absolutely true, and I am going to proceed. The prospectus is so worded that one is forced to the conclusion that the bondholders are getting more or less favoured treatment in respect to class B shares, and that if the general public were allowed to purchase them $60 would likely be the amount that would be asked for them.
The charge made in the house that this company was violating the terms of its lease and order in council is founded on and substantiated by the prospectuses signed by Mr. Sweezey and issued by Wood, Gundy & Company Limited, Dominion Securities Corporation Limited, Robert Dodd & Company Incorporated, and a number of other brokerage houses both in Canada and in the United States.
In these prospectuses it ds made perfectly clear that the plans of the company make provision to take the whole flow of .the river through the company's canal and that work is being done under these plans with that end in view and money being spent therefor. All clearly in violation of the terms of its lease and of the order in council.
I have in my hand a copy of this prospectus issued by Robert Dodd & Company Incorporated, investment bankers, the Royal Bank Building, Montreal. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that it is getting late in the session and desirable that the house should conclude its business as soon as possible. Therefore if I have the permission of the house I will not read the prospectus, but if I have not that permission, then I must proceed to read it, because in it is contained many of the allegations which I made last Thursday, and I am here, sir, to protect my honour. May I have the permission of the house to file this with Hansard?

Referring to the purchase of $30,000,000 Thirty-year 6% Collateral Trust Sinking Fund Bonds of ^ Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited, I give you the following information: Beauharnois Power Corporation Limited has been incorporated under the laws of the Dominion of Canada and is to own or control all the outstanding shares of Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company (which is carrying on the Beauharnois hydro-electric development) and of its associated companies, Beauharnois Land Company, Beauharnois Transmission Company and Beauharnois Construction Company. 
Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company
Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company has acquired under a lease from the Province of Quebec extending to the year 2003, and under authorization from the Governments of the Dominion of Canada and the Province of Quebec, water power rights on the St. Lawrence River about twenty-five miles above the City of Montreal. Its power house, in which it is proposed to install equipment capable of producing 500,000 horse power, will be west of the Town of Beauharnois, on Lake St. Louis. This development involves the construction of a canal approximately fifteen miles in length to the south of the River St. Lawrence, running from Lake St. Francis to Lake St. Louis. Complying with the conditions imposed by the Dominion Government, the canal has been designed so that if the St. Lawrence Deep Waterways project is proceeded with, the canal can be used jointly for navigation and power purposes. In addition to the above water power rights the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company has entered into a contract with Montreal Cotton Company providing for the acquisition of the latter's rights to divert water for power purposes from the St. Lawrence River at Lake St. Francis. In the opinion of the Company's engineers, the water available from the above sources when diverted through the canal will generate 500,000 horse power equivalent to 7,500,000 kilowatt hours per day. Between Lake St. Francis and Lake St. Louis the St. Lawrence River drops eighty-three feet in a series of rapids, making this section of the River one of the most important water power sites in Canada, being capable of developing about 2,000,000 horse power. The average low water flow of the River through this section is approximately 220,000 cubic feet per second. Of this flow approximately 120,000 cubic feet per second is presently allotted to power developments, which amount includes the quantity allocated to the Beauharnois Light, Heat and Power Company. It is estimated that the unallocated balance of about 100,000 cubic feet per second, if passed through the Company's canal, would permit installation of approximately 1,000,000 additional horse power. The Company's proposed development, in the opinion of its engineers, is the most efficient method of utilizing the entire drop in this section of the River. In view of the above provision is made in the plans and considerable work is now being done with a view to installing further units if additional water becomes available. After the completion of the present 500,000 horse power installation it is estimated that further units can be installed at an average cost of less than $65 per horse power. The present plans contemplate that 200,000 horse power will be available by October 1, 1932, at which time the Company will commence delivering the first blocks of power under contracts already entered into, and that the total of 500,000 horse power will be available by October 1, 1935.

175. Section 4 of the report brought in on Wednesday, June 5, 1929, according to the votes and proceedings, contains the recommendation that the said act be amended by repealing section 9 thereof. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that for some years labour bodies all over this country have protested against this section. It is quite easy for great corporations to hide their contributions to campaign funds, and undoubtedly great corporations do contribute to campaign funds in spite of this section. However, this section works a very great hardship on the labour movement in Canada in that it effectively prevents any labour union from contributing to campaign funds. We do not believe this is fair. When the trades unions undertake to contribute to campaign funds, using their money for this purpose in a perfectly open way, it seems only right that they should be permitted to do so.
I think a great many members on both sides of the house will realize the justice of such action as I am proposing. There was one clause
regarding charities which was allowed to stand.

Subsection (j) of section 3
was allowed to stand in order that some decision might be arrived at to widen the exemptions from income tax. The government felt at the time that the exemptions allowed for donations to schools, hospitals, universities and churches went far enough, but during the discussion we realized that there was a great deal to be said for the arguments advanced that this clause might be broadened out in so far as the federated charities, the Red Cross and other organizations were concerned, and we decided that it would be desirable that this clause should be broadened out to that extent. We did not feel that there could be included in this clause definite reference to such organizations as the federated charities and the Red Cross, because we knew that protests would be coming in such as were presented yesterday. In casting about for some phrase which would make this clause as broad as possible, we decided on the phrase "charitable organization," and I propose to move the following amendment:
That section 3 (j) be amended by striking out the words "any church, university, college, school or hospital" in lines 24 and 25, and substituting therefor the words "any charitable organization."
Objections might be raised that the words "charitable organization" would not cover such institutions as churches, universities, schools and so on but I think the hon. leader of the

Income War Tax Act
opposition is familiar with Halsbury's Laws of England in which Charities are discussed as follows:
Only those purposes are charitable in the eye of the law which are of a public nature, whose object, that is to say, is to benefit the community or some part of it, not merely particular individuals pointed out by the donor.
Accordingly gifts which are directed to the abstract purposes of relieving poverty, advancing education or religion, are charitable.
A bequest for the relief of such poor persons as the testator's trustees may choose is charitable, but not where the choice is to be made from a number of named individuals.
"Charity" in its legal sense comprises four pricipal divisions:	trusts for the relief of
poverty, trusts for the advancement of education, trusts for the advancement of religion, and trusts for other purposes beneficial to the community not falling under any of the preceding heads. Within one of these divisions all charities to be administered by the court must fall, though every object which might be brought within one of them is not necessarily a charity.
I submit that this phrase embraces every organization of this kind. The section will then read as follows:
not more than ten per centum of the net taxable income of any taxpayer which has been actually paid by way of donation within the taxation period to, and receipted for as such by any charitable organization in Canada operated exclusively as such and not operated for the benefit or private gain or profit of any person, member or shareholder thereof.

I desire to congratulate
the hon. minister upon having introduced this amendment. I had an opportunity of looking into the authorities after the sitting of last evening and I am satisfied that the term "charitable organization" covers every species of benevolence that any citizen of Canada may desire to indulge in. The limitation not to exceed 10 per cent of the taxable income protects the government and enables the broadest field of choice to the individual who may desire to utilize 10 per cent of his earnings for the benefit of charitable purposes. In fact, the word " charitable" is so broad that there is no field of human endeavour which he may desire to assist that is not open to him.

This is going to give us a
lot of work.
I think not.

Before the bill passes, I do not presume to request an amendment to clause 3, but I should like to direct the attention of the minister to a fact that should, I think, call for an amendment at some future time. I am not referring to my own particular circumstances, although I have two families of
grandchildren dependent upon me. But it has come to my notice that there is a very considerable number of cases in which the father of a family has been killed in the war or has died on account of wounds suffered during the war, and as a result the grandparent has been called upon to provide for young and growing families. Under those circumstances I think the grandparent is equally entitled to and should be allowed the same exemption of 8500 as is allowed in the case of an individual who is supporting a parent, grandparent, brother or sister incapable of self-support on account of mental or physical infirmity I know of some other cases, in which, owing to war service, young men have become not only physically but mentally incapacitated and where the pension tendered in such case by the pension board is utterly inadequate to provide properly for their children's care. I think there should be some exemption when a grand-parent, is called upon to make provision for grandchildren who are suffering under such circumstances.

I should like to congratulate my hon friend upon not pressing the matter at this time. Further consideration may be given to it on another occasion when the act is being amended.

I may point out now that the bill as introduced is somewhat different from the resolution and no doubt clause 2 of the bill was introduced for the purpose of defeating the amendment that I moved when the resolution was before the house. As hon. members are aware, the bill provides for the payment of a bonus to the steel company of fifty cents a ton on every ton of coal used in the manufacture of steel. The object of my amendment was that the money so paid to the company should find its way into the wage envelopes of the workmen. Clause 2 of the bill was evidently framed for the purpose of defeating that amendment. It is nothing more nor less than, camouflage. It is in exactly the same position as the coke oven legislation which was introduced by the government some two or three years ago and which was held out by the government as tending to implement the recommendations of the Dnucan report regarding the establishment of coking plants in different parts of Canada. If there is a law in the province of Nova Scotia and the company does not comply with it, then this government may withhold the payment of the bounty. Now there is no eight hour law in the province of Nova Scotia. Hon. members of this house attach great importance to this eight hour law. I may say that for the men employed in the steel works at Sydney it is not a question of eight hours or twelve hours a day, but it is a question of getting some hours of work. When I was speaking on the resolution I pointed out that hundreds of men had been thrown out of employment, and that others had been given only two or three days' work a week. I gave as an illustration one man who in the past four months had earned only $144. Let this money go into the wage envelopes of the men. Put on a restriction, if you want to, about eight hours, and give them extra pay for extra time; but do not let us try and shield ourselves behind the province passing an eight hour law or any other kind of law.
Has anybody ever considered what the effect of a province passing an eight hour law would be? If Nova Scotia passed an eight hour law covering the industries of the province, say the boot and shoe industry, what would happen? The result would be that that industry would immediately pull out of Nova Sootia and go to some other province where there was no foolish law of that kind. You cannot pass legislation that is going to go up against the economic laws.

I may saj' for the information of hon. gentlemen in the corner to my left that there is a great body of the men employed in the steel works at Sydney who are in favour of protection. It is true that there is a number of them who are discouraged and disheartened, men who have spent twenty-five years of their lives in the employment of that company and who now find themselves no better off than they were when they began. It is only natural to expect in such cases that these ment would be quite content to take desperate chances on ditching the company by denying them any protection at all.
Hon. gentlemen in that corner pretend to be free traders. Let me ask what pressure a free trade government coudd bring to bear on an industry such as the steel industry at Sydney to give their workmen any increase in wages or shorter hours. The only pressure that you can bring to bear on them is the pressure that arises from the protection that you give them. I quite appreciate the fact referred to by the Prime Minister that difficulty would arise in trying to put any such provision in the tariff as was advocated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). But there is no such difficulty with regard to this bonus. This is money that is going out of the federal treasury into the hands of the company, and there would be no difficulty in attaching to it a provision that that money should go to the benefit of the wage earners.
I may say that we had hoped to get a great deal of assistance from this bounty on coal. It is calculated that between four and five tons of coal would go to make a ton of steel, which would mean a bounty of $2 to $2.50 on every ton of steel.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word or two in connection with Ithis subject. At this late stage of the session I shall be very brief. I have listened to two debates on the question of steel bounties and assistance to the steel industry and I do not propose to traverse (the ground already covered. I can say at once that I have every sympathy in the world and I agree fully with the remarks which have been 
made with regard to the men working eleven and thirteen hours in the steel plants. I do not think I can over emphasize that point. What we are considering is the practical situation which is facing this parliament. May I say thalt for the last three years I have been intensely interested in this subject, and I think my colleagues will bear me out when I say that I have not permitted them to lose sight of the fadt that the steel industry of Sydney is a matter worthy of consideration, and I have endeavoured to bring that fact to the attention of the government on every possible occasion. With other members of the house I have realized the difficulties, first with regard to litigation which prevailed, secondly with regard to the situation of the company respecting the over capitalization and the unwieldly organization composed of the large number of companies which were grouped together, some fourteen in number, with a capitalization of over $100,000,000, a matter which seemed to me ought to be Straightened out, and thirdly with regard to the fact that the whole matter was before the tariff board. Hon. gentlemen will remember that we are not simply dealing with the question of a straight bounty; we are dealing with something which will compensate for a rebate of duty. Duties have tc do particularly with the tariff board, and the whole question had to be considered by the tariff board in the light of the application which was being made regarding the tariff on steel and coal. Those matters have been before the board and no one is more pleased than I that the Minister of Finance has been able to bring in a bill to-day in order to carry out the recommendations contained in the Duncan report. I feel sure the explanation given by the Minister of Finance will be sufficient for hon. members of this house who have questioned whether or not this bill carries out the recommendations contained in the report. The present bill does for the steel industry of Sydney exactly what section 1019 of the tariff act does for the steel industry of upper Canada, namely, iit pays to the steel industry of Sydney a bonus of 49J cents per ton for every ton of coal used for coking purposes, and afterwards used for the production of iron and steel. On the other hand the tariff act pays a rebate of 49i cents per ton on coal brought inito Canada and used for exactly the same purposes.
Let me say to the committee that this measure has been urged by everybody in Sydney who could be interested in the matter, lit has been urged by hon. members on the other side of the house. As I have said before it has been urged by me, and I have

Bounty on Coal
repeatedly discussed the matter. It has been urged not simply by those who are in public life but by the associated boards of trade of Cape Breton. I have in my hand a resolution passed by them asking that these recommendations of the Diuncan report be carried out; they do not suggest any conditions, nor do they suggest that there should be any restrictions, bult they simply ask that the provisions of the Duncan report be put into effect. A year ago I had the pleasure of being present when a delegation was received from Cape Breton. Dr. Coadry acted as chief spokesman, and the delegation consisted of men holding different political views and representing various public interests in Cape Breton. That delegation asked that these recommendations be carried out. In addition to that I have had similar representations on behalf of the miners themselves through their president, Mr. D. W. Morrison. I have had representations from the three thousand steel workers asking that Ithis report be carried out, that the tariff recommendations be carried out and that the suggested bonus be carried into effect. In not one single instance has there been a suggestion of a condition being applied in regard to wages or hours of labour.
I had been convinced, and I think other hon. members also had been convinced, that the iron and steel industry might be on the verge of disaster; it was said the industry was going to languish and decline. Those expressions have been used in this house on more than one occasion. That there was danger of collapse of that industry; people were not making large profits, but on the other hand there was the possibility that the whole industry would close down. The object I had in view was to try to help save the iron and steel industry of Nova Scotia. On this occasion we are trying to do that, and we are using this bill to effect that end. As pointed out by the leader of the opposition last night this steel industry has been in the hands of the receivers for the last four years. There has been talk about the profits which have been made; someone mentioned a surplus amounting to about $2,000,000. We must remember however that that $2,000,000 was met by a deficit of about $1,700,000, and leaving a net surplus for the British Empire Steed Corporation, from the time of its organization until the end of last year, of something like $300,000. That is not the type of concern in connection with which it could be said that we are bonusing for the purpose of putting money into -the pockets of the shareholders. The object of this government is to try to put money into the pockets of the workers. The people who
will benefit by the assistance given to the industry will not be the shareholders or the bondholders, but the men who are working in the industry. That is the result which we have been trying to attain. During the last three or four weeks the company has completed a reorganization. As one particularly interested in the province of Nova Scotia and interested- in the iron and steel industry I have scanned as carefully as I possibly could the reorganization proposals which have been published in the newspapers. If hon. members will take the trouble to investigate they will find that several companies with a combined capitalization of something like $100,000,000 have been dealt with so that their capitalization is reduced to about $21,000,000. On the balance sheet the properties are shown at cost at something like $130,000,000. I do not think we can say there has been a very large payment so far as the shareholders are concerned; the bond interest has not been paid for the last four years.
It was -paid last year.

On the two junior issues of bonds there has been no interest paid for the last four years. I am referring to bond interest and not to dividends on shares. That is a resume of the condition of the industry we are trying to help to-day.
As to labour conditions and the statements in regard thereto I wish to congratulate my hon. friend from North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) and his colleague from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in calling the attention of the house to this matter. The remarks of these hon. gentlemen have served to focus the attention of the Canadian people on this matter of labour conditions. I say that these hon. members have done a great service to labour, and in bringing the matter to attention they have done a service to this house. I am not sure my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald), for whom I have the greatest friendliness, can be credited with exactly the same disinterested motives. My hon. friend was good enough to give the government the benefit of his confidence and the benefit of his vote in connection with the budget. I am not so sure the hon. gentleman was prompted by his love for the government, or by the fact that he loved more his seat down in Nova Scotia. He may have been prompted by both motives, however.
I have listened to the debate in connection with this labour question, and I have decided that it has not been an argument in favour of the labouring man so much as it has been a debate between two schools of thought, one
Bounty on Coal

protectionist and the other free trade. I am not concerned with protection or free trade in the abstract in connection with this debate. On the contrary I am more interested in trying to help this industry and to assist the men engaged therein. I would be very much afraid that the labouring men would be crushed between the upper and nether millstones of those who are talking about free trade on the one hand and protection on the other. The workingman would foe forgotten entirely if some of us did not try to stick to the real issue, and the real issue in this particular case is the bill before the house which has for its object the placing of the steel industry on its feet. I want to say to my hon. friends from Winnipeg North Centre and North Winnipeg that since the report to which they referred was made there have been some improvements in regard to the hours of labour. I understand that the mills have come down to ten hours. That may be far too much, but at least there has been some improvement. The continuous operations to which my hon. friends referred, as the hon. leader of the opposition said last night, are still continuing at eleven and thirteen hours, and I agree that such a condition is not good for an industry or good for a country. My hon. friends cannot speak any more strongly on that point than I can, but the question is what to do.
It seems to me that this brings us really to our function in this house. My hon. friend from South Cape Breton, in his second attempt-a rather shrewd attempt and perhaps good politics-sought to focus the attention of the men on himself by moving a rather specious amendment to this bill. What was the amendment? It was that .the whole or a portion of this money should be applied for the purpose of improving the condition of the men. That does not mean anything at all; it is simply eye-wash. The whole or any portion of it means that you could spend five cents, or you could paint some workman's house, and get away with it.
No, not five cents.

The slightest assistance in the world would be enough to comply with this resolution, and my hon. friend would walk out and claim that he had done something for the labouring men of Cape Breton. Let me say to him that I do not believe this kind of resolution means anything except that it means -he is going to endeavour to be the champion of the labouring men down there if he can, but I believe that what the labouring men want is some real asistance to this industry in order .to put it on its feet. under my hand the resolutions to which I have referred, and just the other day, since this discussion came up, I received a telegram which I am going to place on Hansard. At a regular meeting of the general works committee, employees representative plan, Dominion Iron and Steel Company, representing over three thousand steel workers in session this afternoon unanimously decided on the following resolution: We the representatives of the employees of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company Limited do hereby recommend that the budget as handed down be approved without further amendment regarding bonus on coal and tariff on steel. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at one o'clock we were discussing Bill No. 312.

Mr. Chairman, I was
speaking with regard to the provisions of this bill as they concern assistance to be given to the steel industry. The hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) understands the conditions which exist down there, and, as I said before, there is considerable unemployment in that particular section. We are trying to put this industry on its feet and thus relieve some of this unemployment. Some 250 men are employed in the open hearth furnaces, but they are working only about 3i days per week. We feel that that situation should be remedied if at all possible.

Bounty on Coal
I submit that we cannot pass special legislation in respect to one particular industry. Let me remind my hon. friends just what this bill is. The steel industries of central Canada -I group them together-receive a rebate on account of duty which has been levied on coal used in their plants. This bill on the other hand provides that an amount shall be paid to those industries which use Canadian coal.
I find that in the customs tariff there are no less than 50 to 55 items in respect of which drawbacks are paid, and after all this provision is simply a drawback in another form. With this industry in its present condition, this is not the time to propose a principle which if applied at all should be considered in connection with every one of the 55 items, and every one of the 55 concerns represented by those items. This is exactly the same principle which was enunciated with regard to the tariff.
I do not think it is fair to single out one particular industry because it happens to be receiving now what other industries have been receiving right along. So I say to my hon. friends that from the point of view of fairness to the industry, and outside of the question of the position in which it finds itself, I do not believe that this is the proper thing to do.
What we have suggested, and what I believe will appeal to hon. members of this house, is this: If, under the circumstances, the province which possesses the jurisdiction considers that some provision should be passed, not with respect to one particular industry but with respect to all, regarding the hours of labour or the rates of wages, then this government will assist the provincial government in enforcing that law. The law must be made, not by this parliament but by the provincial legislature, and that is the reason for the provision contained in the bill which has been referred to by the hon. member for South Cape Breton as being camouflage. I submit that it is not camouflage, it is a serious effort to put the power of this parliament behind the enforcement of provincial legislation. As has been said repeatedly in this house, the function of the federal authorities will be to pay out the money not to make the law regarding labour, but we will say: If you infringe the laws of the jurisdiction which has the power to make those laws, then in addition to whatever penalty you incur from that infringement we will impose the additional penalty of withholding this bounty.
Reference has been made to the labour conditions in this particular community, and since that time the manager of the company, Mr. Kelley, has made a statement which appears in the Sydney Post of May 23, reading as follows:-
The workmen know that we are behind the eight-hour day move at the steel plant and we have told them that we intend to install that system as soon as practicable. That is, the ten- and eight-hour day or eight-hour shifts for those whose departments are kept in continuous 24-hour operation, and 10 hours in the service departments which are not kept going continuously. At present we are operating the plant on the 10- and 12-hour day system, and it has been our intention for some time past to remedy this condition as soon as conditions improve.
The plant has been through a hard period, and the company have spent considerable in trying to build it up to its proper efficiency. When that is .accomplished the eight-hour day will be established.
The coal bounty, while not as great as might be expected, will help towards bringing about conditions we are anxious to have at the local plant, and we are very thankful for what we have got. It is at least a move in the right direotion.
This is a very important industry to the province of Nova Scotia. I believe that hon. gentlemen sometimes feel that this is an industry situated away down in one end of the Dominion and having to do only with that community. I want the committee to realize that the combined coal and steel industry employs something like 20,000 men; that nearly one-fifth of the population of Nova Scotia is interested directly or indirectly in connection with that industry; that it purchases something like $60,000,000 worth of goods; that it pays out in wages something like $23,000,000; that it pays in Nova Scotia more than 50 per cent of the workmen's compensation assessments being paid in that province. Therefore the prosperity of the steel and coal industry means a great deal for the prosperity of the province. The assistance in the form in which it is granted means assistance not only for the steel industry but for the coal industry as well, because the steel industry uses about one-quarter of the production of the coal mines at Cape Breton, with the result that when you pay a bounty based on coal used for the purpose of making iron and steel, you are giving a very substantial benefit to the coal industry itself.
Let me say one thing more. As regards my hon. friend opposite voting for and supporting the budget, I can quite understand his action when we look over the record of the government with regard to the coal and steel industry in Nova Scotia, and when we see exactly who it is that has done anything to assist that industry. Let me remind my hon. friend of what has been said before, namely, that the

Bounty on Coal

first real assistance to the industry was given in 1897 by a system of bounties which was then put into vogue and which has continued until 1910. Let me remind my hon. friends also that the revision of the tariff in respect of steel, the great revision prior to this one, was in 1907 under a Liberal government. Let me remind them also that slack coal was paying a duty of something like fifteen cents a ton and that it was not a Conservative government, but a Liberal government, which increased that duty to fifty cents a ton because the tariff item regarding slack coal was being used as subterfuge to bring in United States coal and affect the market for Canadian screened coal.

thereupon granted?

This meant that United States bituminous coal could be imported free in the form of coke and it was thought better to encourage the manufacture of coke in Canada.

remembers one that his government put into force since he became a member of it.

The one put through in
connection with salt?

does that affect?

of the thing.

What is proposed with regard to this labour matter is this: we have the announcement of the manager of the steel company and I have read it to the house. Those are the things with which we can go to the men and I believe the men in Sydney know iust as well as anyone what they want and their conditions and perhaps better than even the hon. member for South Cape Breton or any other hon. member. I am content to take their judgment in that respect. I believe they will see through the amendment moved by my hon. friend. It is a life saver, an attempt, as I said before, to indicate that my hon. friend is the champion of the labour men but I do not think an amendment couched in that language and with those nebulous words "the whole" or any "portion" to be devoted to improving conditions, will afford much comfort to the men of Sydney. I believe they will regard the implementing of the recommendations of the Duncan report, the granting of this substantial bounty, the assurance which has been given by the manager of the company, the assurance given by the Prime Minister and the evidence of sincerity which appears in the bill itself as being more calculated to improve their conditions than the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend. My endeavour is to continue assisting this industry to get on its feet. I believe that it can be done. I believe that that industry involves a great deal for the province of Nova Scotia, and I propose when the time comes to go to the men of Sydney and tell them squarely what we have done 2419-172J
and what we are doing, and to present this bill to them as it stands, and I am quite content to abide by the result of that appeal.
I believe that I shall get their approval of what we are now doing and that they will not be misled by the amendment which has been moved by my hon. friend.

I have listened very attentively to the speech of the hon. Minister of National Defence, and with one portion of his remarks I entirely agree. That was his statement .that the amendment moved by the hon. member for South Cape Breton (Mr. MacDonald) would not be of much use as far as the men are concerned. I think that that goes without saying because it is stated in the amendment that a part of the money shall be devoted to the interests of the men. That part would have to be determined by the company, in which event I think that the men would gelt very little out of this bounty which I presume is to be voted by parliament.
With other portions of the remarks of the hon. minister I cannot agree. In his later statements I think he tried to convince the house that the party of which he is a member was a higher tariff party than the Conservative party and he almost convinced me that he was right. I do not know whether in that statement he was voicing the opinions of hon. gentlemen who sit on his own side of the house.
The speech of the minister may be summarized under four heads. He dealt with the bounty on coal; the conditions of the industry; the conditions of the men; and lastly with what the Liberal party has done for the province of Nova Scotia. With the latter part of his remarks I am not going to take issue nor indeed touch upon them but I wish to say a few words in reference to some of his other statements.
The minister said that, first of ah, we should try to put the industry on its feet, and for that reason he thought that it would be unwise to take any action at the present time which would compel the company to give the eight-hour day or higher wages to its employees. Secondly he said that it is not a matter within the jurisdiction of this parliament to say what labour conditions in Nova Scotia shall be, that that was enltirely a matter for the province itself. Suppose that in the near future the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia decided ito put into effect the eight-hour day and insisted on fair wages for the men employed in industry. The whole argument of the minister then falls to the ground because the industry would be compelled bo put those conditions into effect
Bounty on Coal

irrespective of the conditions of the industry itself. The minister shakes his head. If I am wrong I must have misunderstood him. but that is the only meaning that I could take from his statements this morning and this afternoon. He said that so far as this parliament was concerned, we should not do anything that would interfere with labour conditions in Nova Scotia. Secondly he said that it would be unwise to take any such action at the present time because this company and others are taking a sort of fatherly interest in the condition of their workmen, and that if we wait long enough the time may come when the men may receive better working conditions, and therefore it would be unwise, he said, to take the action suggested at the present time. Suppose that the province of Nova Scotia insisted on the eight-hour day and better wages in industry in the province. It would then be just as unwise for the province to insist upon those conditions as it would be for this house. It makes no difference so far as the men are concerned and so far as the industries are concerned where the jurisdiction lies because the law would be effective in any event.
The minister also said that we should not legislate for one particular industry. What are we doing at the present time? Are we not at this very moment introducing legislation for the benefit of one particular industry? Are we not giving to one industry, even to a portion of one industry, special legislation? This bounty is special legislation for the benefit of a portion of the coal industry in the Dominion.

Perhaps my hon. friend did not quite get my point. I was pointing out that this was just one particular industry, and that there were fifty-five others on the books that were getting rebates. This is the same as a rebate, and you could not pick Oiut one industry without legislating with regard to them all.

It is not a rebate; it is a bounty. The steel mills generally buy their coal in the open market and buy to what they consider is their best advantage. But the British Empire Steel Corporation buys coal from its own mines, and we do not know whether they are paying a fair or an unfair price for that coal. But we do know that we have to pay 494 cents a ton to one company under the control of the British Empire Steel Corporation. There is no equality whatsoever in giving a rebate to the steel company at Hamilton and giving a bounty to a company which owns its coal mines.

The Duncan commission
decided the .reverse of that. Sir Andrew Rae Duncan decided that the very basis of this grant was that money was paid out of the treasury to the steel mills of upper Canada, and therefore a like amount should be paid out to the steel mills of Nova Scotia.

I do not accept Sir Andrew Rae Duncan as any authority on this particular question. It was the same Sir Andrew Rae Duncan who stated in his report when dealing with labour conditions in Nova Scotia that the men employed in the mills should be paid according to the ability of the industry to pay wages, and when a man makes a statement of that sort it appears to me that he is not a fit and proper person t6 consider labour conditions anywhere in this Dominion. Wages, irrespective of the condition of the industry should be the first charge on the industry, and whether or not the company can afford to pay good wages is not a matter of primary importance so far as the men are concerned.
I might go a little further. The minister has been very profuse to-day in his declarations about being willing to put the industry on its feet and giving consideration to the industry. I am more concerned, as I have stated on more than one occasion in this house, with giving first consideration to the men.
I said that too.
I want to give first consideration to the men, and secondly consideration to the industry.
I said that too.

But what we are doing at the present time is giving first consideration to the industry, and letting the men take care of themselves.
I am sorry that I cannot see eye to eye with the hon. gentleman who has moved an amendment to the second section of this bill. I have an amendment which I hope to move if his amendment is not agreed to, and perhaps at this particular juncture I may be allowed to state that by my amendment I adopt a portion of section 2 as contained in the bill, but leave out that portion which deals with making this bounty operative when the legislature of Nova Scotia has passed legislation for the eight-hour day and fair wages in that province. My intention is to make this bounty operative only from such time as the industry itself gives fair and reasonable conditions of labour and the eight-hour day to its employees.

Bounty on Coal

I did not intend to say
anything on this subject, but I am prompted to do so after listening to the remarks of the Minister of National Defence, who accused members on this side of the house of playing politics with this question. I am sure that the people of this country, and particularly the people of the province of Nova Scotia, are best able to judge who is playing politics with this question. Going back to 1923, there was then a solid representation of sixteen Liberal members sitting in this house from the province of Nova Scotia. In that year the Conservative party in Nova Scotia adopted the platform of maritime rights, and on that platform they elected the present senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) and thus broke the "solid sixteen." That program was preached by the Conservative party in the two general elections of 1925, with the result that the Liberal party which had held power in Nova Scotia for over forty years was defeated and returned only three members to the legislature. A few months afterwards eleven Conservative members were elected to this house from Nova Scotia. Hon. members know what happened the following year, and they will recall that the Conservative party has advocated that platform consistently up to the present day. The pressure of public opinion became so strong that this government became panicky and in 1926, in the speech from the throne they told us they were going to appoint a royal commission to investigate maritime claims. In due time Sir Andrew Rae Duncan and two associates were appointed and made an investigation. In this they were assisted very materially by the Nova Scotia government of Premier Rhodes, which submitted to the commission a comprehensive brief on the subject matter of the inquiry. Undoubtedly this brief aided the commission in making the report which was submitted to this house in 1926. The legislation now presented by the government with regard to a bonus on steel and coal is based on the recommendations made by the Duncan commission, but although that report was submitted, as I say, in 1926, this government has delayed dealing with them until to-day in the dying hours of the last session of this parliament. I submit that the government is playing politics on this question, not the Conservative party.
The members of the government have pointed out on several occasions that they are treating the maritime provinces very generously and they have called particular attention to the increased subsidy of 8875,000 paid
to Nova Scotia. But the Duncan commission recommended that this subsidy should be paid annually until the proper amount was adjusted, and this adjustment the commission stated should be made at the earliest possible moment. Well, that recommendation was made four years ago, and no adjustment has yet been made. Let me ask the government why?
In this connection I would point out that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) has referred to the bonus granted to the steel companies in 1897. But that was before there was any British Empire Steel Corporation; that was when we had the steel and coal companies in Nova Scotia carrying on a fairly successful business. Because of that fact the money grabbers of this country -the money grabbers that we heard about last week with respect to the Beauharnois deal-saw an opportunity by merging these coal and steel companies into a big organization to make a handsome profit for themselves. They therefore increased the capitalization to such an enormous amount that when they applied to the Borden government for a Dominion charter they were refused. Where did they go? They applied to the old Liberal government then in control of Nova Scotia for a provincial charter, and that government granted the request. I submit to the house that the former Liberal government of Nova Scotia were responsible for the British Empire Steel Corporation and for all the disastrous consequences which have resulted from its incorporation.
There is another matter I desire to call to the attention of hon. members in connection with the payment of subsidies. In the days of the Liberal regime in Nova Scotia we had unrest and disquietude amongst the miners of Cape Breton year in and year out, and strikes were of almost yearly occurrence until 1925, when the Rhodes government succeeded to office. In 1924, the position became so critical that the Liberal government of Nova Sootia applied to the King government to send down troops. This government promptly despatched military units drawn from all over the Dominion and on their arrival in Cape Breton they marched through the affected area with fixed bayonets and loaded rifles the same as our soldiers marched into Germany. What were those troops sent down to Cape Breton for? To threaten these miners who were asking only for fair wages and fair living conditions. In 1925 the federal authorities sent the Rhodes government a bill for the expenses incidental to the movement of those troops.

Before this bill is disposed of I have a very important question to ask the minister and I ask it with some hesitancy. In the Toronto Daily Star under date of May 19 there is a despatch from Ottawa by a staff reporter reading, in part, as follows:
It is suggested in some quarters that Mr. Dunning put the high duties on these commodities to demonstrate to Canada what high protection really meant in dollars and cents on the cost of living. Having plainly shown it, he intends to revise the fruit and vegetable schedule into a moderate tariff.
On May 17, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) sent a communication to various persons in connection with the tariff situation, and among other things on page 4 of his letter he wrote:
In the event, however, of any of these customs duties on fruit and vegetables working out in commercial practice higher than anticipated, they are quite likely to be modified in committee, as in former budgets.

Now, I ask the Minister of Finance, occupying one of the most responsible positions in this country, whether or not there is any foundation in fact for the statement made by the newspaper correspondent and others-some members of this house from Saskatchewan have made a similar statement-that he deliberately introduced into the tariff resolutions a provision with respect to fruit and vegetables which necessitated the payment of high duties, thereby increasing the cost to the consumer, as indicated by the reports made the other evening from Winnipeg and Calgary and other points, and then repealed such provisions and inserted other provisions for the purpose of indicating to the Canadian people that the imposition of such duties involved a higher cost of fruit and vegetables to the consumer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I wish to take only one or two minutes to point out the impracticability of this amendment. I hope my hon. friend will not again reproach me from the point of view of lack of sympathy or lack of knowledge; the question is purely one of practical administration. I think my hon. friends will be kind enough to credit me with having the same sympathy which they themselves have, shown.
The customs tariff is made for use in customs ports of entry wherever they may be, all across this country. The rates set out in that tariff become the rates charged upon imported goods. As I understand the amendment it applies to the whole of the industry engaged in producing the articles named in these four schedules, and it will be noted that in connection with some of them the tariff has actually been lowered, particularly as to the British preference. My point is that at the present time there is one concern, a part of this industry, which has established the eight-hour day with respect to the major portion if not all its undertakings. My hon. friend will see at once the unfairness of the position created by his amendment. If even one of the concerns engaged in this industry did not comply with the conditions of his amendment, assuming it to be passed, then all those engaged in the industry would have applied to their product the former tariff instead of the present one. If industries in the United States were interested in getting their goods into this country at the old tariff rate it would be a very simple matter for them, through the control of one Canadian concern,

Customs Tariff Amendment

to ensure that the new tariff would never become operative; they would simply refuse to comply with the conditions of the amendment. In that way ithe whole Canadian industry might be placed at the mercy of one particular company. I point this out for the reason that again we are attempting to accomplish by indirect means something which we cannot do directly, as was pointed out last night by the Prime Minister. The provincial legislatures can legislate with respect to hours of labour and rates of wages within their provinces. If we tried to do it in the manner proposed by my hon. friend we would simply create a condition of chaos in the administration of customs along the border; otherwise we must apply to the whole industry a condition which is unfair to those of the industry who are complying with the conditions described in the amendment. My hon. friend sees, I am sure, the dilemma from a practical point of view which would arise out of the adoption of his proposal.

There may be some ground for the minister's statement, but I would point out that similar difficulties prevail at the present time. For example, if the Algoma Steel Corporation should undertake to put in the eight-hour day they would be handicapped because of competition with the Besco people at Sydney who would not have the eight-hour day, and thus, for those who want to do the thing fairly, there would be a very great hardship involved. I say that a like situation actually exists to-day which probably is worthy of more consideration than the hypothetical case with regard to which the minister speaks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I can assure my hon. friend that the difficulty created by his amendment would be in fact much worse. I have had it very carefully looked into.

Then further, whilst there might be difficulty with regard to American firms establishing branches in this country, we already have that situation to-day where a great many American firms are actually establishing branches here in order to get in under the British preference. Therefore that situation also is one which at present prevails.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend sees that his own point bears out what I say now. Under his amendment, if one of them refuses to comply with the conditions, he would place the whole Canadian industry under the 
handicap of having imports of these commodities come in from the United States at the old rates instead of at the rates proposed in this tariff. My hon. friend is reinforcing my point purely on the practical side.

I quite admit that practical difficulties are involved, but I want to suggest, as we have been trying to do in several of these debates during the last few days, that practical difficulties exist at the present time so far as the men are concerned. I think I may say the government has done nothing whatever to obviate the practical difficulties that are experienced with regard to labour in the industry, and it proposes nothing to obviate them. Those of us who have been trying to represent especially the interests of labour-because industry has enough people to stand behind it-must do what we can on an occasion of this kind to press again upon the government the necessity of caring for the labour men who are engaged in industry.
This resolution which I have submitted to the committee is almost identical with and certainly follows very closely the lines of that suggested the other day by the leader of the opposition. There are a few phrases which are slightly changed in order to bring it more closely in conformity with the phraseology of the Versailles treaty, that is all. The idea is one which I took directly from the leader of the opposition. From what he said on another occasion this afternoon, in connection with the amendment to the bill providing for a bonus on coal, apparently he feels that under present conditions it is not advisable to force the hands of the company.
I have no qualms of conscience with regard to that at all. The company has been going on for a good many years in one form or another, maintaining these same bad conditions. The fact that it has been reorganized does not seem to me to be a sufficient reason for us to refuse to attempt to safeguard the men at this time of reorganization. Everywhere the interests of capital are given preeminence; in this amendment which I am seeking to have the committee adopt, the interests of the workers are given preeminence and we are making provision that wages and decent conditions of labour ought to be a first claim.
I think I can trust the Minister of Finance so to manage its administration that some of these evils which he foresees might be obviated.

The tariff is imposed for the purpose of providing more work for Canadians in Canada, not somewhere else, and it is believed that this enactment, by increasing the duties on steel 80 per cent, will have the effect of shutting out steel from the United States and enable steel to be made in Canada that heretofore has been made somewhere else. That means that much more work for Canadians who now have no jobs, but to say that the tariff should not apply unless the people in the factories that would be benefited work only a certain number of hours per week is an impracticable suggestion from the point of view of its being carried into effect, because workmen do not import; they only work at new jobs created by reason of this tariff shutting out the importation of steel and enabling the demand to be supplied in Canada.
That is the first reason why I began to study the proposal, but there is a second reason which I commend to my hon. friend. Reforms are not won in a day. The hon. gentleman himself is a striking illustration of that.

The difficulty to my mind
is just this. Section 236 of the act includes advertising, printing, publishing and so forth of information intended to assist in, or intended for use in connection with bookmaking, pool-selling, betting or wagering upon horse races or upon any fighit, game or sport. I do not know whether "sport" would include contract bridge or not. This bill takes out of the general section horse racing. If you are inside the high board fence, you can be shown anything; you may look at the horses and look at the board and see what you want; not that that gives you much satisfaction as i rule, but the information is there available. The only condition is that you must put up your money and get inside the high board fence. People are interested in horse racing aside from betting. Horse racing has been described as the sport of kings, and betting has been associated with horse -racing from time immemorial. This House of Commons has endorsed the practice of betting on horse races. The province from which I come has

also more or less endorsed it and takes a considerable fee from the operations of the betting machines. The betting has become more or less mechanical, and the province profits by -i-t; so that we have endorsed it.
Under the section before us you must not even know a day or so -before a race that a certain horse is the son or daughter of another horse, or what that other horse did in his or her day. That is to say, you are not to be given any information. The newspaper is prohibited from publishing news in regard to a very fine animal because it may be that it would have something to do with betting upon the result of that an-imal's efforts in a race. Then afterwards you cannot go home and tell anybody what the horse paid on a race because you are publishing -information. You go down to the race track, knowing nothing, whether you want to bet or not, because you are not allowed to discuss or read about a horse. You pay your money and get inside the high board fence. You do your betting if inclined that way, and when you get outside you must forget the whole business. It seems to me -that we are being made too good. I am not a racing man myself and am not particularly interested in racing, but I know a great many people who are interested in horse racing and in knowing about the horses, what they do and have done, and in what they did at the races, but under this section when you are going -home on the street car with a friend you cannot even tell him that a -certain horse paid $2.15 on a $2 ticket, because that would be publishing information. The whole -thing is ridiculous. There will be some betting on the election this year, prohaJbly more than on most horses races. There is hardly a member of this house who does not go home in the evening and -play a game of bridge for a small stake, and I do not suppose there is any harm in that.
If you preserve the old provision and require some intention in the publishing, I think you will reach the evil. The police, of course, would like that struck out. They do not like to have to prove things too closely. It is -easier for them to get people convicted when they do not have to prove intent. It seems to me that we are going very far. I know that there are certain papers which are behind this bill and certain papers which are against it. I must say to the minister and to the committee that, after all, no matter how -badly it may be abused, horse racing is a sport in which a great many people in this country are interested, and if the papers of this country are not to be permitted to publish what is perfectly

legitimate news you are clamping on them a sort of embargo or prohibition to which it seems to me a free press should not have to submit.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with section 13 I think we all agree that one of the greatest responsibilities of the state is that which has to do with the protection of children. This section added to the bill will certainly remove the protection all children ought to have in respect to medical care and attention. I have no quarrel with the Christian Science treatment in any shape or form as far as adults are concerned and I do not think members of the medical profession have any such objection. It is not a question of treatment as far as adults are concerned at all; it is simply a question of protecting children, and I object to the proposed amendment as set out in this section.

Mr. Chairman, I
quite appreciate the position taken by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat, but I desire to record my own approval and support of the section for one reason only. I should think that under all circumstances we would view with great hesitation a section of this kind if it were something that dealt with opportunities to be afforded to people who desire to practise in the way indicated for their own personal profit, but it seems to me that inasmuch as the section as it appears in the bill involves the exercise of the practice of a religious belief, the house should entertain the proposal favourably. I cannot see how otherwise we can conscientiously and consistently support that with which I believe the entire house is in accord, namely that every man and every woman shall be free to practise to the fullest extent those religious beliefs he or she entertains. If it were not for that point, Mr. Chairman, I would view the section with considerable disfavour, but in view of the fact that those who are supporting it and those who, I am given to understand, have asked for it, are people who have entertained the proposals as part of the religious belief which they support, I support it. I believe it to be agreed by all members of this house that every man in this country should be free to practise his own religious belief, whatever it may be, without let or hindrance, and therefore I think the house should support this section.

Mr. Chairman, I think
there are some serious objections to this clause at it stands.
