speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Under this section it
would not be a criminal offence under the criminal code.

While it is quite true that .medical men 'themselves practise Christian Science in the cure of patients, down through the years a number of scientific discoveries, such as the one I have mentioned, have been made for the treatment of disease. This treatment might be advised under provincial law, but I doubt if it would be enforced, and the doing away with a treatment of this kind because of religious belief would not be fair to the child. That is the opinion of medical men who know anything about the treatment of disease. The same thing would be true of other conditions such as tetanus. There is a simple preventive treatment for tetanus, which treatment saved probably tens of thousands and perhaps hundreds of thousands of lives during the war.
And typhoid fever.

Perhaps that is not quite so specific an example. Pasteur, one of the greatest scientists of the medical world discovered a treatment for the prevention of hydrophobia. Those are the three distinct treatments which I do not think this house should permit even Christian Scientists, or people of any other belief, to neglect to give to children requiring them from a curative or preventive standpoint.
I remember reading a few years ago of some Christian Scientist parents who refused treatment to a child suffering from tuberculosis of

Criminal Code Amendment
the knee joint. There is a fairly successful treatment for tuberculosis of the knee joint, and not to permit a child to receive treatment because of some religious belief seems to me to be almost criminal. No doubt there are other medical members of the committee who know of scientific methods of treatment for other diseases which are not guesswork or gunshot prescription methods. I wish to place myself on record as being opposed to any legislation which would prevent the proper treatment being given to children who cannot think for themselves. I think it is the duty of those in this house who know something of disease to oppose strenuously this legislation.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to draw the attention of the minister to a few features in connection with this amendment, without desiring to say anything regarding the belief of people who practise Christian Science, or to impugn their sincerity of purpose. A very extended debate would be necessary in order to obtain a full understanding of what this amendment means, but we are faced at once with two or three features. These sections have to do with three classes of persons. The first covers the care of people unable to care for themselves; the second is the obligation of parents towards children under sixteen years of age; but the most important one applies to the guardians of children under sixteen years of age. Those are very sacred trusts, and the bill distinctly says that anything which would tend to produce ill health or death in these particular cases should not be regarded in the light of a crime. Why should one class of people be excluded from these obligations? The bill is discriminatory in its provisions.
The minister says that in the case of diphtheria or smallpox, the provincial authorities can apply quarantine and prevent the spread of the disease. The important point in the application of quarantine is the matter of diagnosis. Who is to say that a child has diphtheria or smallpox? There is only one man can say that, the trained medical expert. Some of the best trained men have been mistaken in the diagnosis of these diseases at their inception. Due to a misunderstanding of all phases of these intricate diseases, they have often swept on and obtained a foothold simply because they were not recognized in time. It is wrong to say that a whole class of a community shall be put in the position of saying that no one shall make a diagnosis or report to the provincial board of health and thereby prevent the spread of disease. The prevention of disease is the result of thousands of years
of observation. The march of science has been going on for hundreds and hundreds of years, and has now reached the point where we are enabled, by applied methods, to save hundreds of thousands from disease and disaster. We are now asked to say that all this accumulated knowledge shall be set aside and that a certain section of the community shall have the privilege of allowing conditions to obtain which we claim should not be permitted.
Take the child who has just died of diphtheria, and let me say that no sadder picture can be presented to the eyes of man in these modern days, than to find again "Rachel weeping for her children" when no warning of disease had been given. There is a child that has died. Somebody had not called in a doctor and the child had not received proper treatment. The persons responsible, in order to escape this criminal action, may plead that they believed in Christian Science and nobody knows whether they do or not until they are charged in a court of law. Some modification must be made in this provision before it is put into force, and to my mind it would be better to let the matter stand over for the present. At this stage of the session this amendment cannot be properly considered and it should be delayed until the members of parliament have had an opportunity of examining into it in all its bearings. I would ask that the minister be fair to men of science, men who have devoted their lives to this subject. At my time of life I am not particularly concerned whether I am called to exercise my function as a physician or not, but as one interested in humanity I would plead with the minister to drop this for the present and if he wishes to bring it up at another session when there will be plenty of time to lay the case before the house and the country, then I am willing to take my chances as to whether this amendment will go through or not.

If I understand this
clause in the bill aright, it means that no one is compelled to call in either a medical man or a surgeon to attend to any case of sickness. If an individual does not call them in. he is not liable for criminal negligence. Many of us who are medical men believe that all cases of sickness and surgical cases should be treated by medical men or surgeons, but there are some of the laity who believe that anyone who is sick or diseased in any way has a perfect right to use his method, whatever it may be. of curing such sickness, or for the
Criminal Code Amendment

treatment of the disease. We shall not find fault with those who take that view, so long as they are at least of the age of twenty-one years of age and of sound mind, if they are willing to lie down and die from diphtheria or appendicitis without calling in a medical man or a surgeon to attend to them. Many people consider that they have a perfect right to do as they wish in these matters, but on the other hand many contend that grown up people who impose their will upon children of tender years who are not responsible for themselves are going too far in deciding not to call in a medical man in case of sickness or disease. I can conceive, for example, a case of a child who has a broken leg or arm. Under this provision it will not be necessary for persons holding the views to which I have referred to call in a surgeon to X-ray that broken limb, see what is the matter with it, and help to set it right. The result will be that the child will go through life crippled and the parents cannot be punished. 1 believe if we pass legislation such as this we shall be liable for criminal negligence ourselves. Nothing could be more outrageous; no one in his senses would think of passing a law such as this.

We have heard
speeches by several medical men in the house on this proposed amendment and they vrould almost give us the impression they are afraid that their craft is in danger; that medical science is going to be seriously interfered with and that perhaps the practice of a physician or a surgeon will be hampered because of the proposed amendment.
Not at all.

We have listened
to several.medical men and the tenor of their remarks has all been along the same line, very strenuously opposed, to the proposed amendment. The hon. member for Springfield mentioned that the object of medical science was the preservation of life. If we are going to carry that through to its logical conclusion, we had better pass legislation that will make it a criminal offence for parents to be neglectful if their children catch cold, for fear that they may get pneumonia and lose their lives. We had better have legislation to make it a criminal offence for parents to clothe their children improperly or under-nourish them. To my mind it would be just as reasonable to have legislation making that a criminal offence as to make it a criminal offence for any person who has a sincere belief in some other remedy, to resort to it.

The object of medical science is to heal or cure any disease. I am not at variance with medical science. I do not discount the ability or usefulness of the doctor. I admit there are cases when the doctor can do work that perhaps it is necessary to have done, but along with that I am prepared to state that there are people who believe they can accomplish more by other means than can be accomplished by medical science. I am not a Christian Scientist; neither do I approve the Christian Science doctrine, but I know personally, absolutely, that we have in Canada several religious sects who practise faith healing. They do so on the basis of the Scripture. They believe what the Bible says. They take the simple reading of the Bible, believe what it says, and when they are sick they call in the elders who pray with them, often with favourable results. The people who are sick are sometimes healed, although not always, but neither are all those who are sick, healed who call the doctors. Sometimes sick people who call in doctors die, but the doctors are not penalized because their patients do not survive. If those who believe in some other method of healing and resort to it, are not successful; if their faith does not reach through, I do not see that they should be charged in a criminal court and penalized.
It would look as though this clause were inserted at the instance of Christian Scientists, but I would judge that it was intended to apply not only to that cult but to people of any religious beliefs or persuasions who care to resort to spiritual means for the restoration and healing of the body. If under the criminal code a penalty is to be imposed on those who resort to other means than medical science for the restoration of health and are unsuccessful it is only reasonable that we should have a premium given to those who resort to other means and are successful. If we have a penalty in the one case, we should have a premium in the other.
Just a few days ago-to be exact, last Sunday-I listened to a gentleman in this city preaching to approximately 2,000 people. He was the picture of manhood and health. Yet he told us that just a few years ago he lay at death's door. His heart was broken down, his stomach had refused to function for months, and his intestines had been paralyzed for eighteen months. He had been under the care and supervision of ten different medical specialists, who had done all they could to restore him to health and had finally given him up. Yet that individual through other means than medical science was restored to perfect health and is to-day a perfect speci-

Criminal Code Amendment
men of manhood. If we allow people to resort to such means as suit them best, I do not think we are violating anything in our legislative enactments. I feel that this amendment is long overdue and that it is something that this house can very well pass.

If this amendment was
confined to grown up people in a normal state of mind, probably we would not find very much objection to it. But there is a duty imposed upon all legislative bodies, and that is to look after the community at large. One of the great objects of the medical profession to-day is not the cure of disease but its prevention. The prevention of disease is the big thing before the medical world today. If you are going to allow people to spread contagious diseases throughout this country without any check at all, I ask the Minister of Justice and the committee, how can you protect the public health? I can give the minister an example from my own experience of a patient who lived in my riding and went to Toronto and died. The corpse was shipped back to Muskoka. I was called to go out thirty-five miles in the country to a lonely part, and there I found ten children sick with malignant scarlet fever, and about three-quarters of them died. That will show you how any contagious disease that is not properly handled and quarantined may produce an epidemic that is destructive to the health not only of the particular family affected but of the public at large. I submit that this house has the duty of protecting the public at large from epidemics that are so destructive to life. I submit, further, that we have no right to allow people to inflict their opinions in these matters upon immature children who have not yet reached the age when they can make decisions for themselves, especially where it is a question of life and death.
This section does not prevent people from employing spiritual means of healing if they wish to do so. Nobody can prevent that. But we do say that people who are responsible for the care of children and those who are not mentally capable of looking after themselves should not be relieved of all responsibility. Less than a year ago I had a case of diphtheria break out in a family, and the father absolutely refused to let me administer antitoxin. Every medical man knows that that is the best and practically the only specific treatment that we have for diphtheria, and if given early enough it will save probably nine hundred and ninety-five cases out of a thousand. I had to report the father of that family to the Minister of Health at Toronto
in order to bring pressure enough to bear so that those children could be properly treated. If I had not done so, the disease might have spread to the six or eight other children in the family and might have cleaned them all out. When we get a case of that kind we not only treat the patient but administer antitoxin to every child in the family.
I ask the Minister of Justice, is he going to lift the responsibility from everybody for maintaining public health and taking care of immature children and others who are not capable of making decisions for themselves?
I submit that this section is dreadful. I submit, further, that it does not prevent anybody from using spiritual means if they wish to. But people should not be relieved of all responsibility in these matters, and I ask the Minister of Justice very seriously to consider withdrawing this section altogether.

I am a little astonished
that the Minister of Justice should have allowed himself to be inspired by some such deceptive spirit as must have taken possession of his soul when he conceived this amendment to the criminal code. I thought that the Justice department was quite alive-it should be-to the benefits that can come from the judicious application of science, but in this amendment I see an inclination to efface at one stroke all possible succour to people who through ignorance of their own state of health or through an ill-disposition towards others would put the life of the community in danger. I do not look upon this as a question of faith and morals; I look upon it as a matter of the public weal.
I was rather amused at the hon. member for Kindersley reflecting upon the medical profession, fearing that they might lose a patient or two. I would tell the hon. member that if his craft or that of any other member of this house were to carry on its practice with the same abnegation that characterizes the medical profession, people might be a great deal better off and suffer much less. There is too much of a disposition on the part of the laity to ignore the benefits that accrue from medical science. In France formerly there used to be such an amount of charlatanism practised that Moliere in many of his writings makes the physician appear ridiculous, and many people from reading his works are inclined to look upon the medical profession as being influenced more by suggestion than by action. But, Mr. Chairman, we must awaken to the necessities that surround us. We must safeguard our own interest in so far as our community life is concerned. I can readily imagine persons suffer-
Criminal Code Amendment

ing from tubercular disease of the lungs taking no precautions simply because of ignorance. I can conceive of a person suffering from a mild attack of smallpox walking about the community without the disease being recognized-as was the case, I may say, in Montreal some years ago. On that occasion over a thousand lives were lost because the necessary precautions were not taken in time. This is not a matter to be trifled with at all, it is of most serious moment and I hope that the minister will see the advisability of withdrawing the clause.

Mr. Chairman, I am free to admit that I expected opposition to this section, though not perhaps to the extent that it has developed. My reasons for inserting the section in the bill are to a large extent those which have induced my hon. friend from West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) to support it. During the last few years it has been represented to me that an exception should be made in this case. Since this bill was introduced I have received hundreds of telegrams from all parts of the country congratulating me on this section and urging that it be passed. They feel very deeply- and I can assure my friend from St. Ann (Mr. Guerin) that they are intelligent people and belong to all classes in the community-they feel very deeply that their moral obligation to provide necessary treatment for their children should not be placed in conflict with a legal obligation in a certain way which according to their conscience and even to their religious conviction is not the best form of treatment.
I may say that one of the principal reasons which influenced me is that such an exception is recognized in some way or another in the legislation of almost all the provinces. In Alberta, for instance, the law defining and regulating the practice of medicine provides that:
Nothing in this act contained shall apply to jr affect those who practise the religious tenets of their church without pretending a knowledge of medicine or surgery, and provided that the laws, rules and regulations relating to contagious diseases and sanitary matters are not violated.

Any child may be apprehended as a neglected child "whose parent or guardian neglects or refuses, when able to do so, to provide medical, surgical or other remedial care necessary for his or her health and well-being."

speechtext: However, this is the first time that a section of this nature has 'been placed before the house, and I think in justice to those who have urged the amendment it is well that it should have been presented to hon. members. We have heard the arguments against the clause, and I am pleased indeed to have received the support of my friend from West Hamilton and my friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). Mr. Chairman, I entirely agree with the minister's decision to withdraw the section, and I congratulate him upon his decision. But I think a word should be said in reply to what I think wias an

Criminal Code Amendment
unintentional but uncomplimentary remark by my hon. friend from Kindersley. I have the utmost respect for him, largely because of his general fairmindedness upon all questions that come before the house, but he unconsciously, I am confident, twitted a profession which for centuries has been noted throughout the world because of the fact that its practitioners regard all questions concerning health from the public standpoint. I will give my proofs of that in fairness to the large body of medical men in Canada, thousands of whom have sacrificed much of their time for charity. Every advance in the practice of medicine and surgery-and advances have been made in practically all the civilized countries of the world-has been placed at the disposal of humanity free of charge. Take for exam/ple, the outstanding discoveries which I have jotted down from memory while the minister was speaking. The discoverer of anaesthesia was a Scotchman, Simpson; of antiseptics, Lord Lister, an Englishman; of antidiptheritic serum, a Japanese; of hydrophobia serum, Pasteur, a Frenchman; of Salvarsan, Ehrlich, a German; of insulin treatment for diabetes, Banting, a Canadian. Not one of those men-and I name only six that came to my mind as I listened to the minister-patented his discovery or derived any monetary advantage from it. I should have made one exception, but I will not mention his nationality. And by the way, our present Deputy Minister of Health is a man wlho bears an outstanding reputation in this country. I was glad to have the honour to assist in his appointment some years ago. Practically all the advances in public health have been made by mediaal men and it has been pointed out on many occasions that because of the advances they have made in public health they have been depriving themselves of their own livelihood. Without wishing to delay the committee further may I say that I think the remarks I have just made are due to a profession which certainly deserves to be numbered among the noble professions of the world. I am sure my hon. friend from Kindersley will be one of the first to acknowledge that in my remarks I have merely done justice to the profession.

I think the hon.
gentleman has read into the few remarks I made much more than was placed in them or was ever intended to be placed in them. I am of the opinion that the hon. gentleman has been much more generous towards the profession which he represents than he has been towards .the religious sect to which I referred during my remarks.
Section 13 withdrawn.
On section 14-Evidence in trial for manslaughter through negligence.

Sections 14 and 15 in this bill make such drastic changes in the criminal law that I feel it incumbent upon me tc take a few minutes of the time of this committee to point out, particularly to the members of the committee who have not legal training, what the effect of these proposed amendments will be. For this purpose 1 think it is necessary to state that section 261 of the criminal code, which section 14 oi this bill purports to amend, is the manslaughter section, and section 284, which section 15 purports to amend, is what is commonly known as the criminal negligence section of the criminal code. Section 284 reads:
Every one is guilty of an indictable offence and liable to two years' imprisonment who, by an unlawful act, or by doing negligently or omitting to do any act which it is his duty to do, causes grievous bodily injury to any other person.
It has always been one of the basic doctrines of our criminal law that before a man can be found guilty of a criminal offence there must be mens rea or a guilty mind. May I point out to the lay members of the house that this does not mean that the crown must read the mind of a man who stands before the court? Where, however, a man has been guilty of a wanton disregard of the rights of others a guilty mind or wrongful intent is properly inferred by the court, and he becomes guilty of a criminal offence. Under the section which is proposed the merest civil negligence plus physical injury resulting in death would make a man ipso facto guilty of manslaughter. The same mere negligence plus physical injury, but not resulting in death, makes a man guilty ipso facto of a criminal offence punishable by two years' imprisonment. I fully appreciate that this amendment was designed to affect the drivers of motor cars, but on careful analysis it will be found that the section is more far-reaching in its effect. To illustrate I shall point out one or two instances which have come to my notice.
A returned soldier who had lost an arm at the war was appointed as a gatekeeper at one of the Toronto railroad crossings where then is a great deal of shunting of trains. Tht man's duty was to raise and lower the four protecting gates at the crossing when th* trains were shunting in the immediate vicinity. On the occasion in question he managed to lower three of the gates and had lowered the fourth one from a perpendicular position to a position half way between perpendicular and horizontal when a motor car travelling down
Criminal Code Amendment

the street went through the gate. A section of the gate touched the top of the motor car when it was passing through. The result was that a shunting freight train struck the motor car and the two occupants were killed. Action was brought in the civil court against the railway company and the jury found negligence. As a result the railway company had to pay damages. On the other hand the gatekeeper was charged with the criminal offence of manslaughter, but the charge was reduced by the crown counsel to an offence under section 284 of the criminal code. Under our law as it then stood, there not being such a degree of negligence as to amount to a wanton disregard of the rights of others, he was found not guilty. Under the proposed amendment however that man would be ipso facto guilty of negligence.
Not at all.

My hon. friend says "not
at all." I could illustrate further, but I do not wish to take up the time of the committee by considering in detail the circumstances connected with the leading decisions handed down by our appeal courts of Canada for the last five or ten years.
I shall state another illustration. A farmer and his hired man went into a field to load turnips, and) the farmer drove the horses up to the fence. He and the hired man loaded the turnips, and at the conclusion of their task the hired man was not feeling well, and for that reason he leaned against the tailboard of the wagon with his head resting on his hand. At that time the employer stopped and chatted with him. At the conclusion of their conversation the farmer left the hired man leaning against the tail-board and climbed on to the wagon. With the intention of backing up the team in order to turn them he seized the reins; as a result the team backed up quickly, the man was knocked over and the hind wheel of the wagon went over his leg. It was found that the leg was broken and in the court the farmer was held civilly liable in damages for negligence; because as an ordinary, reasonable and prudent man he should have looked around to see that the hired man was not in the position in which he had left him before he pulled on the reins. Under the proposed amendment I most seriously submit that the man is ipso facto guilty of negligence.
One of the hon. members from the city of Winnipeg who is at times rather dogmatic in his opinions is now of the opinion that I am wrong in my deduction. I shall read (Mr. Lawson.]
the new clause proposed to be enacted by section 15:
When any person is charged under the provisions of this section with causing grievous bodily injury to any other person by doing negligently or omitting to do any act which it is his duty to do, evidence which is sufficient to establish negligence upon the same facts in a civil case shall be sufficient for the conviction of any such person so charged.
I submit to the hon. members of this committee that it does not require a gentleman of legal training to inteiipret that section. It is perfectly obvious that, if it is passed, mere negligence plus physical injury ipso facto amounts to a criminal offence, and under section 14 mere negligence plus physical injury resulting in death ipso facto makes a man guilty of manslaughter. I for one, sir, as a lawyer who has had some little experience as crown counsel and also in defending some of those charged under the criminal code, cannot permit these sections to pass without registering my strenuous protest against any such legislation.

Everyone knows that
sections 284 and 285 of the code, which for some years have been the law of Canada with regard to motor accidents, are too uncertain and inconsistent to secure a verdict in any court in this country. I am surprised at this late stage of the session the minister should bring down a makeshift amendment like this. He 'has had recommendations from many of the ablest judges in the land as to how these sections might be strengthened. One of the judges refers to these amendments as tinkering with the sections, whatever that means. Section 285 is pooriy worded; in the dying days of parliament a short time ago the words " by wanton or furious driving, or racing, or other wilful misconduct, or wilful negligence " were added. That has given reason for some of the judges to hold that in no case can there be criminal negligence unless it is of the peculiar character set out in the words quoted.
We have a large department of justice here; surely they can bring this law u.p to date. This country is miles behind the mother land in law reform. There is no law reform in Canada at all; a grand jury is not allowed to go into one of our federal institutions, and the officers of the crown are to be judge and jury and everything else. In my opinion the present department needs to get some modem ideas instead of living in the dead text books of the past.
The proposed amendment to section 284 is clearly illegal. The hon. member for West

Criminal Code Amendment
York has referred to one particular case. In the case of Rex vs. Palmer it was stated in the English court of appeal that there must be some quality of mind expressed in the act of the person before there is a criminal offence, in the absence of wilfulness and recklessness.
In my opinion the minister has not touched even the fringe of the subject. This matter was before the house on March 4 last, when I quoted the opinion of the Chief Justice of the Common Pleas for Ontario, given at the London assizes. He said:
And as now nearly everyone is a car owner and car driver, young and old of all sorts and conditions, it is difficult to get justice in even a civil action. Car-driver-jurors have nearly all the speed fever; and self preservation instincts are so strong that they will not be persuaded to decide against drivers who have been no more unlawful than they themselves often, if not commonly, are.
What then is the remedy? I think it should be: make the laws plain and reasonably severe and enforce them; and cancel licences freely.
And at the other end of the matter: Give no licence to anyone who is not proved to be mentally and physically7, and from experience and a knowledge of the highway laws, thoroughly capable.
The amendment proposed now will mean nothing; it will simply lead to more chaos and confusion than there is to-day along the lines I have stated. The same judge suggested that the words "with negligence" might be added to section 284, but that suggestion has not been adopted either. In England they appointed a committee of both houses of parliament to consider these questions. I have before me the evidence which was taken and the changes which they made to their law. On March 7, 1930, the report was presented to both houses of parliament and a bill was introduced known as the road traffic bill which contained 82 pages dealing with the whole question.
Last year there were 72 people killed on the highways of Toronto through the negligence of automobile drivers. Have the public no right to use the streets; are they to be killed off in this manner? Four times as many people have been killed on the highways of Toronto as were killed at the battle of Queenston Heights many years ago, but here we have a department of justice to which recommendations have been sent by judges all over the country and as far as I can see they are simply pigeonholed. If the minister wanted to be progressive and do something for the public safety he should have appointed a committee of both houses to consider this matter and bring in a proper bill. At the present time a judge can tell the jury that 2419-174
there is no definition of negligence under the code. It is enough to make more judges write letters to the newspapers.
Just here I might quote a paragraph which appeared in the English Review of April, 1930.
It is as follows:
Lord Hewart, Lord Chief Justice of England, has recently published a book under the title The New Despotism. The book is an important one, both because of the high office of its author and because of its subject. Lord Hewart has, quite rightly, refused to accept the idea that a judge is, to use his own words, "condemned to a lifelong and compulsory silence upon the affairs and the interests of the state." The country should be grateful to him for this book and for his criticism of an undesirable but growing tendency in public affairs. His theme is, in the vvords of his publishers, the exposure of "certain tendencies and methods which threaten to impair the
reality of free institutions	Government
departments secure to themselves power to make rules, orders, and regulations without any real and effective control on the part of parliament. They obtain for their orders the force of statutes, and prevent their decisions from being reviewed by the courts of law." The tendency has been developing for a generation at least.
The Minister of Justice has been in England; I think he might have learned something aboi.it law reform there. There is no provision here to take care of the hit and run driver, the most cowardly person in the world, who knocks down some little child and then gets away before anyone can catch him. The Ontario Safety League has made recommendations as to how these sections should be strengthened; why did not those recommendations receive some consideration? I introduced a bill last March to amend this section, defining reckless driving and injuring persons by negligence, having to do with hit and run drivers and so on, but I was unable to proceed with it.
There is another matter which might have been considered by the minister in connection with these two sections; I refer to the recommendation of the Chief Constables' Association. I read last February of a case which was brought uip at a meeting of that body, where a poor farmer of Tecumseh, in the county of Essex, was injured by an automobile, in which accident his wife and children also sustained some injuries. The driver of the automobile was an American, who said he lived somewhere away down in Ohio. He paid a small fine and got away, and as a result the farmer was out of pocket for the injuries sustained by himself and his family, which cost him something over $700. They had first to find the man, but he had given a wrong name and address. The constables'



Criminal Code Amendment
association has recommended that in such cases the driver shall be required to give a bond or put up some money before he is permitted to leave the country. Are we to have the children of this country knocked down in this manner?
The Minister of Justice has said that this is a matter of civil rights and comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces, but it is nothing of the kind. I submitted these proposed amendments to one or two of the judges in Toronto who have had considerable experience with this class of case, and they were not in favour of them. The first amendment dealing with the evidence in a trial for manslaughter is clearly illegal, and should it pass the section of the criminal code will be still more inconsistent. The only way to stop this maiming and killing is to impose a stiff penalty and treat them all alike, both high and low.
The code should contain some provisions as to who shall and Who shall not drive a motor vehicle. These matters should have been brought before parliament earlier in the session. For the past five or six years these amendments have been brought down during the dying days of .parliament, they are hurried through this house and sent over to the Senate. That is not the way to protect life and property on the highways of this country. The time has come when something will have to be done. In my opinion, the minister should appoint a commission composed of three or four judges to consider the present inconsistencies in the criminal code. The way the law is to-day, the public is not protected. A man can knock down another man and kill .him, obtain bail and be tried for negligence, and in ninety-nine cases out of one hundred he will get off. This matter has been the subject of inquiry by coroners' juries, by judges and by grand juries, and it is considered to be a menace and peril to the country.
It would be far better if these sections were not amended, because they are made still more inconsistent. It is hard enough now for a judge to know what is meant, without adding further inconsistencies. The practice which prevails in England should be adopted in this country, and the bill should be circulated throughout the country and criticism and discussion invited thereon. This haphazard method of bringing in amendments should not be allowed to continue. A word is changed there, a comma is added there, and the result is more disorder than ever.
	, *

Mr. Chairman, I
desire to add my protest to that already voiced by the hon. member for West York (Mr. Lawson) against sections 14 and 15 of this bUH. It will be noted that in each of these sections the test of criminal liability is the giving in court of evidence sufficient to establish negligence, upon the same facts as in a civil case. I cannot say what effect that will have in some provinces, but in the province of Ontario its effect would be rather disastrous and its application would be most [DOT]onerous and unreasonable.
For example, in all cases governed by the Highway Traffic Act of the province of Ontario, where a pedestrian is struck by an automobile, the direct burden of proof is put upon the driver of the automobile to establish that he was not negligent. If the wording of the present proposed sections were made applicable, it would mean that every motorist would have cast upon him the burden of establishing his innocence in a criminal charge brought under these two sections. That is absolutely repugnant to .the spirit of British justice and fair play. It has always been conceded that whatever burden might be cast upon a man to show himself innocent in respect of any difficulty in which he was involved, should be a civil condition only, and no man should ever be put in the position of having to prove himself innocent of a criminal offence.
In the province of Ontario, and perhaps it is common to other provinces, we have certain by-laws which, having been passed, are invested with the force and effect of statutes. For example, there is a rather general provision that certain municipalities may designate what are known as stop streets. If a man passes a stop sign and enters on to a through street, he is adjudged guilty of negligence. Shall we say *that such a man becomes a criminal under the criminal code in like circumstances? That would be the necessary and inevitable effect of the passage of these two sections.
There are many cities which have enacted by-laws providing that certain motor vehicles must not approach nearer to the curb of the street than five feet. Shall we say that the man who operates a motor vehicle which strikes someone who is within four feet of the curb is a criminal, but the man who strikes someone within five feet and a half of the curb has no liability? That would be the only possible effect of the adoption of sections 14 and 15.

Criminal Code Amendment
It has become a matter of litigation in our courts as to whether or not civil liability attaches in cases of breach of that section of the Highway Traffic Act which provides that every automobile must carry a tail light visible at a certain distance to any other motor vehicle or a vehicle of any kind atpproaching it from the rear. The Supreme Court of Canada has found itself unable to solve that question satisfactorily-I refer now to the Hall versus Guelph case-as to whether or not there was negligence in the case of a man who operated a motor vehicle which had its tail-light burning in compliance with the law when he started on his trip but the tail light of which had gone out without his knowledge before he concluded his trip. That was the decision in the case to which I have referred and which went through the Supreme Court of Canada. Under this provision shall we say that a man who starts out with a light properly equipped, who has made every test for safety to himself and the rest of the travelling public, shall be made a criminal because the lamp which he has properly lighted has gone out without his knowledge before the conclusion of his trip? Under sections 14 and 15 of the bill, that would be the inevitable result for him. The only possible effect of embodying in our criminal code those provisions to which I now allude would be the unfortunate one of making the laws so onerous, bear so hardly on innocent men, that juries would refuse to convict. We have seen enough of that sort of thing from what happens south of the line. We do not desire that our criminal laws shall bear so severely that people will resent the spirit of them and refuse to enforce them in the courts of the land. I ask the minister to give this matter further consideration. He knows I am making these suggestions to him earnestly and to the best of my ability and I trust he will pause before proceeding further with these two sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
These two sections have been inserted in the bill to meet the demand of the authorities of Ontario; as a matter of fact it is the Deputy Attorney General of Ontario who has been insistent on what he claims to be the need of improving the law in this regard. As the opposition to the bill is so strenuous, and coming especially from my brethren of the legal profession in Ontario, I am quite willing to withdraw the two sections.
Sections 14 and 15 dropped.
On section 16-Driving while under the influence of liquor.

I do not want to be in the position of opposing every section in the bill, but may I direct the attention of the minister to the tremendously far-reaching effect of the amendment proposed:
Every one who, while under the influence of intoxicating liquor.
The minister is probably well aware that the old section read:
Every person who is intoxicated.
By a series of decisions those words have been defined. We know what they mean. Now we bring in a much wider term '"under the influence of intoxicating liquor." Has the minister considered what that term means? I presume, from a physiological standpoint, I am now under the influence of a glass of wine that I had with my dinner.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend would be.

Perhaps on account of the
sensitive nervous system of the Minister of Justice, he may be under the influence of a glass of wine he had with last night's dinner.
I would respectfully ask: Is there any advantage in this change, which is bound to cause a tremendous amount of confusion, a change which creates a new term which has not been defined, although the law seems to be very well and strictly administered under present provisions by our police magistrates and fully covers the case of a man who is in charge of a car while intoxicated?

I would point out that by
adopting such legislation as this we are subordinating our jurisdiction to that of any one of the nine provinces that might be so unwise as to pass some foolish law. I am quite sure the Minister of Justice has no intention of placing the administration of justice in criminal matters under the jurisdiction and power of any provincial legislature.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am quite willing to
restore the word "intoxicated" instead of "under the influence of intoxicating .liquors," if that meets the views of my hon. friend.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The other amendment, paragraph (a), is asked for by the prosecuting authorities of the province of Ontario. I suppose there is no objection to that.
I have none.

There is some
objection to that.

Criminal Code Amendment

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that the word
"intoxicated" be substituted for the term "under the influence of intoxicating liquors." That will make the clause read as it was formerly.

The minister is about to
amend the first part of the section, putting the law back as it was before. I have a good deal of sympathy with the proposal as drafted, but I have no strong opinion on the subject and I am not going to oppose what it is proposed to do now. With regard to the penalty, I agree there is necessity for increasing the penalty in these cases, but greater discretion should be placed in the hands of the magistrates. My experience is that these cases usually come, on summary conviction, before a police magistrate. As paragraph (a) is now drafted, the minimum is thirty days. It seems to me that the magistrate should have a discretion up to a maximum and a smaller minimum. That is the suggestion I have to offer to the minister. Imprisonment for three months is a pretty stiff penalty for driving a motor car while intoxicated. My suggestion to the minister is that that be left as the maximum, but that the minimum be reduced.

I have a good deal of
sympathy with the bill as originally drafted:
Everyone who, while under the influence of intoxicating liquor or any narcotic, drives any motor vehicle or automobile.
It is recognized now that alcohol and high-powered motor cars make the worst kind of combination, and it has been shown conclusively that the man under the influence of the first drink is perhaps the most dangerous. The most dangerous man is not the one who is completely incapacitated. The most dangerous one is the one who perhaps thinks he is in a position to act quickly. Anything that destroys a man's ability to act quickly, perhaps by just a fraction of a second, makes the difference between an accident and safety. Just as the man who has taken one or two drinks is a bigger nuisance than the man who is dead drunk in the gutter, so it has been pretty conclusively proved that thie most dangerous man on the highway is the one who has had just enough not to incapacitate him altogether, but to destroy his ability to act quickly in an emergency. For my part I am willing to have the law made as severe as possible against the man who, having indulged in intoxicating liquor, undertakes to drive a motor car.

As regards the proposed amendment, I think the section as drafted is altogether too severe. Under these words "or has the care or control of a motor HVfr. H. A. Stewart.!
vehicle or automobile," there have been in Montreal cases where people have been compelled to go to gaol. I remember one instance in particular of a man who came out of a club and stepped into his motor car. He felt that he had been imbibing too freely to drive the car. He sent down to the garage to get a helper to come up and take his car to the garage, but when seated in his car, waiting for the helper, he was arrested by a police officer and later sentenced to gaol. Is that justice? I know of another case of a very prominent Montreal doctor who came out of a private house and as soon as he came out some person had in the meantime reported him as being intoxicated. He stepped into his car in front of the house. He was then arrested by a couple of police officers, but fortunately for him, in some manner or other, he got out of it. But that is the law, and it seems to me that it is not the right kind of law to have on our statute books. Under the section, if a man has "the care or control of a motor vehicle whether it is in motion or not," if he should be even found in his car, harming nobody, but just sitting there realizing that he is too intoxicated to drive his car, and he sends for another man to drive it, he has to go to gaol if some police officer comes along and arrests him; and they call that justice. I cannot see it. Personally I think the clause even as it stood before the proposed amendment is too drastic. It is not the kind of law that any Canadian citizen should be subject to and condemned to a gaol sentence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I must say that up until this evening I have always been receiving complaints and representations that the law concerning motor car accidents was not strict enough. Complaints come from everywhere that the law should be made stricter. As far as the clause referred to by my hon. friend is concerned, it is already in the law, and I am not changing it at all. The only change that I was proposing was to substitute the words "under the influence of intoxicating liquor" for the word "intoxicated." This has been requested by many people, but in view of the objections I have withdrawn it. So far as paragraph (a) is concerned-
I find that paragraph (b) covers the point that I had in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, and I will give my hon. friend the reason why it is there. As it is, if a man is prosecuted for having caused bodily injury, the jury cannot convict him for any lesser offence, but with this amendment the offence may be reduced to the one provided for in section 16.

Criminal Code Amendment
Then I have no objection.

I think there is some objection to the choice which the prosecuting attorney will have. On a certain set of circumstances one prosecuting attorney may decide to proceed by way of indictment; on the same set of circumstances another prosecuting attorney may decide to proceed by way of summary conviction, with very different results in the two prosecutions. It seems to me that the object could be accomplished by increasing the penalties but not leaving it open to the prosecuting attorney of his own motion to decide which course he shall adopt, whether to proceed by indictment or by summary conviction. We have a similar provision, as I recall it, in the Narcotic Drugs Act, where for a very serious offence, posibly long continued violation of the law, there is the right to proceed by indictment, whereas in the same act there is the right to proceed by way of summary conviction. It seems to me this is leaving the door open to possible abuse by a prosecuting attorney who, even with the best of intentions, might in one case to-day decide to proceed by way of indictment and to-morrow proceed by way of summary conviction, with very unequal results to t/wo offenders who are really guilty of the very same offence.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I am afraid that the object which we have in view cannot be achieved otherwise than by this means. As I stated, it is to enable the court to reduce the offence if it believes that the charge of causing bodily injury is rather too serious a one for the case. It could not be reduced to an offence punishable upon summary conviction. I think my hon. friend understands what I have in mind. I really believe that this will be an improvement.

Let us assume that the prosecuting attorney decides to proceed by way of indictment. Do I understand the minister to say that upon a prosecution by way of indictment we can come down to the penalty .that is imposed under paragraph (b) for summary conviction?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No.

That cannot be done. So it all depends upon the whim or the decision of the prosecuting attorney whether on the same set of circumstances a man shall incur a penalty not exceeding three months and not less than thirty days, or whether he shall incur a penalty not exceeding thirty days and not less than seven days -very different penalties for what after all
is the same offence. I have great reqpect for the prosecuting attorneys of the province of Ontario as I know them, but it seems to me that .this is placing them in an unfair position. It is placing upon them the burden of deciding in a particular case against a particular individual whether to proceed by indictment or by summary conviction. We do know that all culprits may not look alike, may not be of the same standing, may not appear to the county attorney in just the same way; but it does seem to me that as this is drawn it is bound to result in inequalities and in some cases in injustice, or at all events it will gave rise to the feeling that someone else has had a much better deal an the same set of circumstances.

This particular section
might just as well be withdrawn too. Only the other day a small newsboy, nine years of age, crossing the highway to sell a man a paper was knocked down. I have a list here of twenty-six juries which presented recommendations last year for more drastic laws along this line, and if this is the bc-st the minister can do, I suggest that he withdraw the section altogether. He might as well present these offenders with a watch and an illuminated address.

Section agreed to.
Sections 17 to 38 inclusive agreed to.
On section 39-Shorthand notes of proceedings and evidence.

During last session I brought to the attention of the Minister of Justice the question of amending section 236 of the criminal code, under which agricultural fairs are allowed to operate games of chance, and the minister promised to give it his attention at this session. I have read the bill but I fail to see any section for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In what way was my
hon. friend suggesting an amendment of the section?

In section 236 the minister
will note that a special privilege is granted to agricultural fairs to operate games of chance on their grounds. This is an offence if practised elsewhere. There is a very strong feeling in western Canada that this privilege should be withdrawn, because agricultural fairs are primarily conducted for the purpose of developing agriculture, and the federal grants made to those fairs should be used for educational purposes. We find that the farmers' sons instead of devoting their time to the judging of the stock and getting the
275S
Criminal Code Amendment

full educational benefit from it have their attention distracted by these games of chance, the proprietors of which make a handsome profit without giving any corresponding benefit in return. Resolutions have been passed by our local organizations asking that this section be amended so as to prevent gambling at these fairs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not know whether
my hon. friend was a member of the house when this amendment to the criminal code was enacted a few years ago. I am almost afraid that my colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is largely responsible for it; it was asked for by the Department of Agriculture as a means of encouraging agricultural fairs. The amendment was debated by the house at considerable length before it was adopted. I would not feel at liberty to propose any change at the present time, but I shall be pleased to submit my hon. friend's request to those who asked for that amendment.

I have also had a large number of requests from fraternal organizations, as I believe have several other members, asking that this privilege be extended to them. Personally I am in favour of withdrawing the privilege from agricultural fairs; but if this is not done I see no reason why a similar privilege should not be extended to the fraternal organizations. If the minister will not consent to withdraw this privilege from agricultural fairs, I would ask if he can give any good reason why it should not be extended to fraternal organizations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
My only good reason is
that I have always thought an amendment of this kind would have no chance of going through parliament. As far as I am concerned I am free to admit to my hon. friend that I would have no conscientious objection, or in fact any objection, to the change that he proposes; but when the section was first discussed in the house there was a strong feeling against extending facilities for these games of chance. However, if my hon. friend could persuade me that a majority of the house would support his request I would have no hesitation in helping him. But I think the whole thing should be carefully considered, and perhaps we might postpone such consideration to a future date.

I would suggest to the
Minister of Justice that if he is going to continue to the patrons of agricultural fairs the privilege of spending their time and their

money trying to find which shell the pea is under, and that sort of thing, he should take into consideration the desirability of seeing that no previous knowledge is given of the game and that the winning odds are not published afterwards-precautions that apparently he thinks so necessary in other cases.
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Section 11 was allowed to stand.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, at the request of my hon,. friend from West York (Mr. Lawson).
On section 11-Broker reducing stock by selling for his owm account.

Mr. Chairman, this section, I believe, was recommended by the conference of attorneys general, with the exception of the representative of the province of Quebec who, I understand, did not take part in it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that so?

That is my understanding. The object of the section was to prevent brokers selling stocks short. I realize that in the present state of public opinion it would be a hopeless task for me to advocate its withdrawal. However, I do want to put myself on record as being opposed to it in the interests of the public themselves, but I am not going to take the time of the committee to advance any argument in that regard.
I wish to draw the attention of the minister to the words in the latter part of the section:
-if the effect of such sale shall otherwise than unintentionally be to reduce the amount of such shares.
And so forth. That phrase is unknown in all our legislation with respect to criminal offences. I would submit that, instead of the words "otherwise than unintentionally" we should use the words "with intent," which are always employed in connection with criminal offences. I asked to have the section left over because of the very able argument advanced by several hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house when we were dealing with the criminal negligence section that there should be intent in order to constitute a criminal offence. Now I submit to the minister for his very serious consideration the substitution of the words, "with intent," for the words "otherwise than unintentionally." The minister will no doubt be concerned as to whether the public would be protected if these words were changed. May I point out to him that every province in the Dominion of Canada, with the exception of the province of Quebec, has now adopted and enacted a uniform act known as the Security Frauds Prevention Act,

Criminal Code Amendment
for the control of the brokerage business.
In section 21 of that act is contained the very provision which is in this code making it an offence under the provincial statute punishable by a minimum fine of 81,000 and an optional imprisonment of six months for a first offence. In addition thereto under the provincial legislation there are additional clauses which give to the customer of any brokerage house the right to repudiate his entire transaction with that house and to obtain his money back if the broker is guilty of making a short sale. That is what is intended by the section. As I pointed out, the proposed section goes much farther. For instance, if I am a director of a large brokerage house in Canada-and I have in mind one of those houses with twenty-six or twenty-seven branches-because I happen to be a director of the concern, although I may take no part in its operations,
I am prevented from making a short sale in the market. It may be that some customer of that brokerage house in New York city has purchased a stock of the same class and kind that I as a director am selling short on the Canadian market. As I said, I realize that it would be unwise under present conditions to ask that the section be withdrawn. I feel however that the minister will agree that we should preserve that which has always been a cardinal principle in our criminal law; there must be intent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I appreciate the viewpoint expressed by my hon. friend, and I take this opportunity to congratulate him on the clarity with which he has discussed this bill.
I feel sure that he will understand my position when I say that we have thought it better to adhere to the language suggested by all the provinces. There may be two or three words which we would have liked to change, but I think on the whole it is advisable to leave the section as the provinces have desired it to be left.

On March 4 the Minister of Justice promised that when this bill was presented I would have an opportunity to bring in one or two amendments, and on that occasion he asked me to let my amendments stand. In Ontario some of the judges have apparently disregarded the respective rights of judge and jury. In some cases the judges have made comments on the verdicts rendered by juries, and have made unfortunate remarks in regard to the way the juries dealt with the evidence before them. With these facts in mind I think some amendment should be made
to the criminal code. I would suggest the following amendment:
It shall be the duty of the presiding judge to record and enter the jury's verdict without comment thereon.	.
This is a practice which has become prevalent throughout the country, and as a result it is difficult to obtain men to serve on jury panels. The functions of a judge are defined by law; they are set out by precedent and by statute. There is no legislative authority for a judge to criticize the action of a jury. He sits in the capacity of a presiding judge; both judge and jury have functions to perform. I think however that at the present time the judges are going altogether too far, and this applies to some of the recent appointees in the province of Ontario. They are overstepping the line which separates the function of the judge and that of the jury. I understand there are some common law references to this matter; the English judges do not attempt to encroach upon the duties of the jury, and in my opinion Canadian judges should take a similar attitude." In fact, under our wonderful new status, now that we have a status of our own, I doubt very much if the judges should be addressed as "my lord'' or "your lordship". I understand all these old obsolete laws have been repealed, as have been the forms and usages in connection with them. Something should be done by the minister to check this growing practice of invading the rights of the people. In my opinion judges have no legislative authority from this parliament to make either favourable or unfavourable comment in connection with a verdict once it has been rendered by a jury. With these facts in mind I ask the minister to accept the amendment I have proposed. In the province of Ontario the jury system has been assailed by three or four judges. I shall not take the time of the house to give details, but I wish to say that their remarks have been entirely out of order. I would like to know whether the minister will accept the amendment or whether it is his opinion that anything should be done in connection with this important question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am afraid the suggested amendment cannot be accepted. It almost amounts to a reflection upon the judges. Apart from that I think the judges have a right, if they wish, to send juries back to reconsider their verdicts. I wonder how a judge could take that action without first addressing some remarks to the jury. I do not think the proposed amendment can be considered.
Criminal Code Amendment

Very well, I shall withdraw the amendment, temporarily.
Amendment withdrawn.

The subject matter of the second amendment is contained in Hansard of March 4. In amendment I move that the following words be added to section 41:
The grand jury of any county in which a penitentiary is situated may visit, view and inspect the same and make a presentment of any recommendation they see fit, notwithstanding the provisions of the Penitentiaries Act, chapter 154 of the revised statutes of Canada, 1927, or of any law, custom or usage to the contrary.
This matter is referred to in Hansard of March 4. Within the past few days public attention has been directed to the case of two young boys who were sentenced to imprisonment in one of these institutions, and it has been proved that they were wrongfully sent there. I wonder if there are any others like them down there. How many great penal institutions are there in which innocent people are incarcerated. In Hansard of March 4, 1930, I find the following:
In Hamilton, two sane men for several years were in the asylum and in one case in York county girls were found without food and shelter, in a dungeon below ground, this being a punishment for some minor offence. The chief justice in addressing the grand jury said: "I am in accord with your views as to inspection of these penitentiaries. Such inspection is in accord with that great principle in the administration of justice which for centuries has been applied and was confirmed by Magna Charta, namely, that the people shall have a large share in the administration of justice in criminal cases.
Whether penitentiaries are well or ill managed they are managed altogether by crown officers; and the management of them is a thing of much importance in the administration of the criminal laws so much that assuredly the people should be entitled to some means of learning for themselves what the crown officials are doing and how if is being done.
The grand jury, representing the people of the judicial district, can most conveniently, and at no cost, perform for the people the duty of visitation.
. but one matter of detail I mention, because it seems to me that it should receive consideration.
. f'1 some counties there may be five grand juries in a year. Let me suggest that their Power be limited thus: say twice a year."
These institutions have been managed by the crown and while there is no complaint as to the way they have been run I think it is in the public interest that they should be visited by the grand jury. The minister has said these are provincial institutions, but that is not so; they are established under the criminal code, and the officials are appointed by this government, which maintains the

institutions. No one knows what is going on there. Are there any more innocent people in these places and, if so, how did they get there? It is the right of the grand jury to go through provincial institutions in the same way. There was a big fire in one of these places across the border a short time ago because the proper inspection was not carried on. Are we just to take some person's word for it that everything is all right? We will have more reforms if we have the grand jury go to these places once or twice a year and make a presentment to the court. The grand jury represents parliament and the people; it is an old institution and should be allowed to go through these places and make inspections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has proposed an amendment of this kind where, if it should be desirable, it should be made; that is, to t'he Penitentiaries Act. That amendment did not meet with favour in the house, and properly so, (because after all provincial institutions must not be under federal control. Our officers have no jurisdiction in the provincial gaols, and grand juries, which are provincial bodies, do not have and should not have jurisdiction in federal institutions. Why should the grand jury in the county of Laval have jurisdiction over the penitentiary at St. Vincent de Paul, when the other grand juries in other sections of the province would have no such jurisdiction? Why should the grand jury of Fron-tenac county have a special privilege or duty with regard to the penitentiary at Kingston which would not belong to the other grand juries in other sections of Ontario? I do not think the amendment is workable; it has been debated in the house and settled.
Amendment withdrawn.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
house adjourned while we were discussing the amendment to the motion to go into supply,
I had been speaking with reference to it. The amendment was to the effect that immediate steps be taken to implement the

Peace River Railway-Mr. Mackenzie King
pledge alleged to have been given by the Prime Minister at Edmonton in November, 1924, with regard to the Peace river outlet, and as I recall it the alleged pledge was to the effect that this outlet should be decided upon and a railroad constructed as soon as was humanly possible.
If I remember correctly I had mentioned that at the time of making the speech referred to, I had said that so far as the government was concerned we were confronted in this parliament with, to say the least, some uncertainty as to what might be possible with respect to railway legislation, inasmuch as some of the railway legislation which we had introduced had failed to pass the other house and we were without a majority there. However, this evening I do not wish to delay the committee, and perhaps I can satisfy my hon. friend as to the government's intention in the matter if I say to him that since this amendment was introduced I have had a personal interview with the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Minister of Railways and Canals has interviewed the president of the Canadian National Railways. Both presidents agree that in their view it should be possible for some appropriate outlet to be agreed upon within a period of possibly six months, and I understand they have their surveyors at work with a view of determining a suitable route.
The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company mentioned that a joint survey of the natural resources of British Columbia had been undertaken last year at the expense of the government of British Columbia, the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which was done in consequence of a suggestion made by him to the provincial authorities. It is expected that the result of that survey will shortly be made available. Not long ago the provincial government asked that the work should be continued to include the Peace river block recently transferred from the Dominion to the province, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways each undertook to pay one-third of the expense. When the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company was in the west last fall with the directors of the company he gave an assurance that this year the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would undertake a detailed survey of the possible routes for the outlet with a view to ascertaining which was the more feasible, and also to settle the question whether a crossing of the Peace river at Hudson's Hope can be made. The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company mentioned to me, in the course of
our conversation, that he thought this work should be completed within the course of the next few months, and he stated also that he felt that he and the president of the Canadian National Railways should be able to get together and decide upon the route. He was of the view, which I understand is held also by the president of the Canadian National Railways, that the work should be undertaken jointly.
Now, Mr. Speaker, may I repeat what I said the other evening, that in the opinion of the government it ought to be possible for these companies to agree upon a route within six months and to have work begun within a year on a railway which will afford an outlet from the Peace river district to the Pacific. I will say that if they do not make a beginning within a year and the present administration should be in office at the end of that period, we will undertake to find a way or make it for the beginning of the construction of a railway line from the Peace river district to connect with the Pacific via some other railway line or otherwise. Under these circumstances, perhaps my hon. friend will feel that it is unnecessary to press his amendment any further. I said that the government would accept his amendment. To accept an amendment to the motion to go into committee of supply may seem contradictory, but I was anxious that the government should not be put in a position of appearing in any way to be unwilling to implement to the full any promise which has been made, either directly or indirectly. I hope that what I have said will be satisfactory to my hon. friend.
Mr. BRADS': The right hon. the Prime Minister realizes the importance of having a survey made and he states that within six months there should be definite information at hand as to what is to be the outlet from the Peace River district to the Pacific coast.
