maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE

speechtext: Indians-Ontario and Quebec, $448,485.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the total vote for Indians in Canada amounts to over $5,000,000. I have not one word to say against the administration of the Indian department because I believe that the minister in charge and his deputy are doing everything possible for the welfare of these people. 'However, has not the time come when we should consider the Indians of Canada as being no longer wards of the government? These boys and girls are given a fairly good education, taught a trade, and they leave the reservation and should be permitted to grow up as we grow UP, to become real citizens of this country. In the county of Renfrew we have an Indian reserve. During the past five or six years many boys and girls have left that reserve after having been educated, rightly so at the expense of the government, have gone out into the world and have made good. If 
we could arrange that Indians throughout Canada could receive an education or training in a trade and the government would keep on placing these boys and girls where they should be placed, surely at the end of at least a generation we might be saved a great deal of money which we are spending from year to year. This money is often spent very foolishly. Indians who have lived on the reserves return there, many of them living absolutely in idleness, depending on the few fish they may be able to catch or the few game they may be able to corral. If the government would take this matter in hand, the time would come when these large amounts, like the $5,000,000 that we have been asked to vote to-day, would not be required and the Indians would be as good people as any others in this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
If these Indians wore
good enough to serve in the great war in large numbers, why are they not good enough to receive the citizenship of this country? While we are bringing in immigrants from all over the world, the red man hias no rights in Canada. His rights, privileges, and land are taken away from him and the agreements we have made with him are being broken.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
My hon.
friend surely does not appreciate the fact that the Indians happen to be the wards of the government and they are so by treaty. We have to deal with a situation that came about by the evolution which took place when the white man came and established himself in this country, and out of that grew the system of placing the Indians on reservations. Year by year I frankly confess that I have strongly advocated larger expenditures of money on these people.
May I say to the hon. member for South Renfrew that we are doing a great deal of work in educating the Indians. In this regard much credit is due to religious organizations that are carrying on this work. Possbily it would not be carried on so reasonably as it is were it not for the fact that they do the education work. We have been providing, during the last five or six years since I came into my present position, the necessary schools and equipment for the education of the Indian children. The department have lent every assistance possible towards educating and encouraging the Indians to take enfranchisement and to become citizens in the real sense of the word. That is not urged upon them, but it is a privilege they may accept if they are in a position to do so. Therefore in every way we are endeavouring to educate the

Supply-Indian Affairs
Indians and I should like, if funds were available, to carry the work even further, to give technical education, to train these young boys in trades after they secure, as they do, a good common school education in their own schools in every province. But this will require more money. Year by year we have to vote more money. Since fur has become so valuable in this country and the white man has become active in trapping animals and securing their furs, it has been much more difficult for the Indians to obtain a livelihood. For that reason we have to spend more money on them, for relief, for medical attention and for what, undoubtedly, the country and the government owe to our aborigines. I believe we are not spending enough money upon the Indians, but I realize one must keep within reason in asking for the necessary funds to carry on this work. We shall, however, have to spend more money in giving the Indians better medical attention in the future than we have done in the past and I make no apology for asking these sums of money for Indian work in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Can the minister give any information as to the intention of the government with respect to the erection of a new building to replace the old Shingwauk Home building?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE

I am sorry
my deputy is not with me at this moment, but I may say that we are as quickly as possible replacing old buildings with new and modern ones, and erecting new buildings where they seem to be required for Indian educational work. My deputy will be here in a few minutes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
They are carrying on at
present in a building that has been in existence for a period of upwards of fifty years. It is not modern at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I have it in mind. I cannot say whether it is in the program for this year or not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I would like to refer to the question of the fire extending from the Indian reserve at Fort William into the park. The minister is quite familiar with the facts and it is some time since I put them on record in a letter to him. The minister's deputy takes the attitude that the parks board which asks for assistance in the putting out of that fire has not a just claim inasmuch as the Indian department, although admitting that the fire started on the reserve, contend that they have already spent, I think, some $3,500
in assisting the Indians in fire protection. I am informed that $3,500 was spent on an absolute necessity in the shape of fire protection which should have been put in long before, and it has no effect so far as past accident is concerned. I wish, without delaying the committee at all, to impress upon the minister once again what I have done in private and by letter, namely, that I believe the parks board, which has had a very difficult time getting along and which has suffered because of the fire extending into their park from the Indian reserve, should be given consideration by the minister and some assistance towards at least the expenditure made by them for the upkeep of the volunteer fire fighting force-it is only a matter of about $700-should be given by the department of Indian Affairs, in spite of what my good friend the deputy minister states in regard to the matter. I trust the minister will look into this once again and endeavour to see that the parks board receive this assistance. It can be done without delaying the matter at the moment and without any special vote. I presume there are in the Indian department as in other departments votes out of which a sum of $700 or $800 could be taken. I am not speaking for what little political effect this might have; I am speaking very seriously because I think the parks board have a just case. I feel the minister thinks they have a just case and I hope he will see they are given some assistance in regard to the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am familiar with the subject the hon. member has brought up. It is one upon which we have not reached decision. I have had inquiry made and I may say the report is not particularly favourable, but I think my hon. friend is correct in saying there may be some claim and I will look into the matter again.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think in this case the minister's deputy is a little too economical for the department and he should let down the gates in justice to the parks board of Fort William.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words about this item. Lest it be taken for granted that we approve these votes, I desire to point out to the minister that during the last, few months, in fact during the last year, I have received very serious complaints respecting the administration of the Indian department in western Canada. The fault does not rest with the officer immediately in charge, political patronage has played a large part in the matter, in which the deputy head is wholly without authority. For instance there
27G4
Supply-Indian Affairs

have been eases of machinery bought merely for .the purpose of providing business for friends and which lies outdoors unused. In one instance the minister employed as farm instructor to the Indians an undischarged bankrupt, and in another case a man who is addicted to the use of liquor to too great an extent was put in a position of authority with the result that at times he gets under the weather with injurious consequences to the Indians.
There is a vast sum of money being expended for the Indians,. and this talk of the minister about his desire to help these wards of the nation would sound better if he would give some little expression to that sentiment in concrete form in a proper expenditure of the money voted for the purpose, and with less exercise of political patronage in the making of appointments. The Civil Service Commission which makes appointments in some cases should make them in all. It is not simply one case; there are three cases in particular. Why is it that the near relative of a member of parliament is taken from Portage la Prairie and put on a reserve? Did the Civil Service Commission approve of it?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Under what circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I cannot tell my hon. friend.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I think the minister
could if he took the trouble to. The people in that locality at all events think so. In one instance the Indians were moved off one reserve-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Where was
that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Not far from Portage,
and they are supposed to be removed to another place; I do not know whether they have been or not. This is the report that was made by a gentleman who went through the west, a gentleman with no political bias at all, but with the one object of seeing how the aborigines were treated. He inquired why farm machinery should be left lying around unused-mechanical power for farming purposes unused. He also saw this reserve that I mention. In fairness to all concerned I am leaving out the name of the particular individual, the minister having ample opportunity to investigate these matters, lest it be said that injury is being done to any particular person.
Some years ago the idea was started that the Indians were raising very large crops. For instance, in my own province of Alberta there 
were the exigencies of-shall I say?-the demands of friends that reserves should be leased near Macleod; then reserves somewhere else; then the sale of the lands of a reserve east of Calgary; and when you go into Saskatchewan you find difficulties of the same sort, especially in the northern part of the province; and as well in Manitoba. The result is that although it is said that the Indians are producing large quantities of grain, in the main it will be found that they ate not making the progress they should for the moneys that are expended, and part of the moneys we are expending belong to the Indians. There is a vast fund in this country that belongs to the Indians; for when lands are sold which the Indians own the proceeds from the sale of these lands goes into a trust fund the income of which is available for the maintenance of the Indians.
I have referred to three reserves in Alberta. I refer to a reserve in Saskatchewan. There is also a reserve in Manitoba, the Long Plains reserve, which I mentioned a little while ago. The Indians I referred to are the Indians who were removed from Portage to the Long Plains reserve. I could go into these matters in detail, but I think it is sufficient for my purpose to indicate them lest it be said that we have approved of this vast expenditure; and I say "vast" advisedly, because while it may be a relatively small sum of money, actually it is a very substantial sum. You have $2,500,000 out of $5,000,000 being used for Indian education, including the construction of school buildings. It would be desirable, if we had time, that we should have a complete statement from the minister as to just what work is being done and what the results are. Possibly the nearness of the end of the session is a good reason for not wanting to go into the matter in detail, but I should like the minister to know that there are those deeply interested in these questions who are studying them from outside observation, and they believe that the results obtained are not at all in keeping with what could be secured from the expenditures made. A tendency is manifesting itself to expend money in the purchase of facilities for fanning which are not used for farming, with resultant idleness on the part of the Indians-the tendency of the Indian in that direction is well known to all-with the unfortunate result that instead of the Indian becoming more self-respecting he is becoming more dependent. Occupying as they do very excellent areas of land of high agricultural value, we know that there are not wanting those who are always endeavouring to see that these lands are sold

Supply-Indian Affairs
and purchased by someone else. The minister has had a good deal of experience in that regard in various sections of the country. He knows the means that are taken to have the Indians made to believe that it is desirable for them to sell, and then when they find their reserves gone and the lands sold the result is that you have a worse condition than you had before. The minister knows the difficulties which sometimes have been pointed out in correspondence from, I fancy many others besides myself.
Without taking the minister's time or the time of the committee to go into the mass of detail which I have under my hand, and which I had expected would be useful at this session of the house, representing accumulated detail extending over twelve months, I do suggest to him that whatever little time he may have at his disposal for Indian affairs might be utilized in having the closest possible inspection made of all the reserves in the western provinces. I know the inspectors' reports. Unfortunately I have seen some of them and have checked them up. I know the difficulties in connection with farm instructors, and I am not unmindful of the difficulties which the minister has to experience with those who think that they are fitted by a kindly Providence better to discharge the duties of instructors, farm and others, to Indians than any other people in the world. But if we are to get some value for the money that we are expending and make the Indian, as we all desire to do somewhat more selfreliant and less dependent and improve his position in the community by encouraging him to engage in agricultural pursuits and the raising of stock, as was done at one time in connection with two reserves in Alberta, we shall have to adopt different means from those which are now in vogue. I know not whether it is so or not, but certainly an authority to whose judgment I attach a great deal of importance is strongly of the opinion that there has been a steady deterioration in recent years in the morale of the Indians upon the reserves. That is not wholly attributable to my hon. friend's administration, of course, but it is attributable to causes which the government might, it seems to me, by taking strong action overcome. I content myself with pointing out these matters, without taking time to read a vast quantity of evidence which I have dealing with them. I ask the minister to endeavour to ensure by-shall I say?- observation and action on the ground, and not departmental action from Ottawa, that better results are obtained for the money expended than those which we have heretofore
realized; for some of the education that we have given the Indians has only resulted in the poor unfortunate becoming the easier the victim of the tendencies of modern civilization.
I think the minister knows what I refer to in that regard. Despite the efforts that are made to prevent the Indian becoming the victim of drink, very often his improved education has the more readily made him the victim of shall I say?-civilization. All these things are matters that I regard as of great importance from the standpoint of the treatment of our aborigines, and I earnestly hope that steps will be taken to improve the conditions I have mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
There are
reserves in western Canada-I presume my hon. friend is speaking of the farming reserves -where implements are left out of doors. But that is the case on almost very farm in western Canada. On the whole I think we have more facilities on the Indian reserves for storing agricultural implements than will be found on ordinary farms in any given locality in the western country. As fast as we can get money-because after all it is a question of money-we believe in providing facilities for covering these implements at or near the agent's quarters on the reserve. The appointment of agents is made by the Civil Service Commission, usually after a competitive examination.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It was not agents that I mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Farm instructors are appointed by the commissioner at Regina. The case mentioned by my hon. friend is that of Mr. Edwards, who, he says, was an undischarged bankrupt when he received his appointment. I did not know anything about that at the time. After his period of probation he did not prove to have the necessary qualifications for the work and he is no longer in the employ of the department. My hon. friend says that the Indians are making no improvement in the way of farming. May I direct his attention to the Blood reserve at Macleod? They had well over one hundred thousand bushels of grain on that reserve last year. The Indians on the Blackfoot reserve are also making progress. As to the sale of Indian land, I agree with everything my hon. friend has said. Usually the reserve covers the best land in any given locality, and there is a desire on the part of the people who surround it to secure that land and they try every means in their power to get possession. The Blackfoot reserve was sold long before I became Superintendent
Supply-Indian Affairs

General of Indian Affairs, and we have had a good deal of trouble in getting collections of the moneys due the Indians, but we have succeeded in straightening out the difficulty. It is not the policy of the department to sell any land required now or that may be re* quired in the future by the Indians of western Canada if it can be utilized by them for grazing, agriculture or any other purpose'.
With respect to the education of the Indians, when I took charge of this department I found the various churches of the country, the Roman Catholic under the Oblate Fathers, the Anglicans, the Presbyterians, the Methodists-of course the Anglicans and the Catholics were engaged in this work to a much greater extent than the Presbyterians and the Methodists- I found that these churches had constructed buildings and had become responsible for the indebtedness incurred in their construction, and they were levying upon their adherents to secure money necessary to carry on their educational work. These churches had gone into the country in a missionary spirit to educate and christianize the young Indians, and I did not think it was fair to have them carrying that heavy financial burden. Therefore I immediately took steps to purchase from them the institutions that were considered to be useful for a number of years to come and to replace as far as possible the structures that had fallen into disrepair. To-day the churches are carrying on their work under much better conditions than they did when I became minister of the department.
With 105,000 Indians scattered over the Dominion from the Atlantic to the Pacific, and away up in the Arctic, it would be Strange if some of our officials did not go wrong once in a while. But may I say to the hon. leader of the opposition that I will not tolerate an official on an Indian reserve who has anything to do with liquor-and I am not a prohibitionist.

maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
maintopic: SUPPLY-PEACE RIVER RAILWAY OUTLET AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is one very strong resolution I have made in this regard, and I intend to carry it out. So far as I know, we try to keep the staff engaged in Indian work as reasonably clean as we possibly can. I do not say that we will not have difficulties now and again; anyone who has to administer this department is bound to have difficulties; but I say we are making progress, and did time permit I should be glad to inform the house of the lines along which we are making splendid progress in Indian affairs.

my department received a letter from my hon. friend. I made inquiries, and as a result I find that there were statements made to the effect that this man was an undischarged bankrupt. I wish to move that this
house do not adjourn at eleven o'clock tonight.

speechtext: We should have a definite statement as to when the house will rise. We had difficulty on one occasion in connection with that matter and it is better to have a definite time to take the place of eleven o'clock rather than to proceed indefinitely and then have difficulty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SITTING THIS DAY AFTER ELEVEN O'CLOCK- SITTING ON ASCENSION DAY
speechtext:
My hon. friend and other members of the house are no doubt aware that to-morrow is Ascension day, and that in the past it has not been customary for this house to sit on that day. It has not been customary either to sit on May 24. As we had two sittings on that day and are now doing our utmost to get through with the business of parliament as rapidly as possible, it might suit the convenience of all if we were to meet only for two sittings tomorrow instead of three as we are doing at present. In that way we would leave the morning clear and meet in the afternoon. If that is agreeable, I would suggest that it might be advisable to meet at the hour of two o'clock in the afternoon instead of at three o'clock.
In regard to this evening, I imagine it will meet the convenience of all parties if we fix the hour of adjournment at one o'clock. Some hon. members have mentioned that we might continue to sit until two o'clock; on the other hand, I have learned that there are other members who prefer to adjourn at one o'clock. That being the case I would suggest the hour of one o'clock, and with the consent of the house I shall include that hour in my motion.

I want to bring to the attention of the minister the matter of some Indian accounts. In softie instances in the province of Saskatchewan Indian agents have gone out to the farmers and purchased seed grain, feed oats, hay for horses and in some instances cattle. In some cases these people have received part pay, but in others they have not received anything. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister last year, and my remarks are recorded at pages 3807 and 380S of unrevised Hansard. Among other things the minister said:
In every case where he is able to .produce such an order we are prepared to settle, and in some eases where the evidence is clear that the transaction actually took place and that the creditor has given value for the claim, we will try to make an adjustment.
It seems to me that some provision should be made at this session of parliament to pay these accounts when the agents get seed grain or feed from farmers. I hope the minister will see that these accounts are paid this summer.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
All I can say is that we do recognize the orders of the agents, but we do not pretend to recognize trading done with Indians unless by the
276o
Supply-Indian Affairs

authority of the agents. We have had a great deal of difficulty in settling up old accounts which have dragged on for some years; many of the obligations in this respect occurred during and just after the war. 1 think, however, with the exception of just one or two at Touchwood we have paid up most of these accounts, and the crop on the Blood reserve this year will no doubt clear up a very heavy indebtedness which exists there. We are watching the matter very closely and hope we will be able to clean up the last of these acoounts before the year is over.
Am I to understand that it is not the intention of the department to take care of these accounts at all until such time as the money comes from crops belonging to the Indians themselves?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: No, that is not what I want my iron, friend to understand. As far as possible we want to avoid taking money from our Indian account for the purpose of paying these amounts. In the case of the Blood Indians there was about $50,000 owing, a very large amount, and I am informed that this year their crop will clean up that account. In some cases we have had accounts long overdue and have had to vote the money to pay for them. I want my hon. friend to understand that it has not been an easy task to clean up this old indebtedness, but I say we hope to be .able to clean it up during the present year.

I should like the minister to understand also that it has not been an easy task for these men to carry these accounts for ten or twelve years, some of them for very large amounts. I do not refer to any cases where trading has been done between the Indian and the farmer;
I refer to cases where the agent went out and gave orders on government stationery. The farmer, thinking he was going to get his pay in the near future, let go of a valuable liquid asset and still has not received his money. We make loans to harbour commissions and many other institutions throughout Canada, and it seems to me this matter should be cleaned up now. It should not be difficult to make a loan to the department which would enable these legitimate accounts to be paid. They should be paid; it would not take a great deal of money and it would relieve a great deal of hardship among the farmers who have been carrying these accounts for a long time.

I have quite a large file of correspondence here in reference to the case of C. B. Rothery, who was a clerk in the Indian office at Onion Lake. This man claims to have been unjustly treated; he was appointed to the position through the Civil Service Commission, and after six months probation he was dismissed by the department. I have a recent letter from him in which he says:
A communication from J. C. G. Herwig, service bureau, Canadian Legion, to the representative of the imperial section of the Legion-a copy of which letter has been passed to me-reveals the following interesting admission by the Indian department:
"We have been met with a bland denial of such interference (political) and been told that the department did not wish to accept Rothery in the first place, doubting his competency." This I consider explains the attitude of the Indian department throughout the whole business and does prove their intention to appoint the nominee of C. R. McIntosh. M.P.; further that it certainly supports my contention that they did not intend that I should get past the period of probation.
And so on. I also have a number of communications from prominent people in the district, which I will not take time to read bo the committee. However, there is one letter from a prominent gentleman in Fort Pitt, Saskatchewan. I will let the minister see this letter if he wishes, but I do not wish to put it all on Hansard or to give the name of my correspondent. I should like to read a short extract, however, as follows:
The whole district feels most strongly about his dismissal from the position he held as clerk at the Onion lake Indian agency, a feeling I certainly share myself. We all know Rothery as a very capable, courteous man fitted in every way for the position he held at Onion lake. His academic qualifications and experience place him right in the front rank, and it is disgraceful to think that he should have been dismissed from Onion lake on such paltry grounds. I have gone into the whole matter most fully, and to me the business will hardly bear the light of day.
We all feel that Rothery was eminently suited for the job as clerk at Onion lake. His past records are irreproachable. I have made a number of private inquiries into this matter and have viewed all possible aspects of this case. I now come to the conclusion that there should be a thorough, impartial inquiry into the whole business, which I know would lead to Rothery's reinstatement.
Would the minister care to make a statement in connection with that case?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Yes. I may say that I have heard of this case to-night for the first time, but I am informed that this man was selected by the Civil Service Commission for the position; he was taken

on for a period of probation of six months, and was found to be unfitted for his job, so he was let out. As I say, I had not heard of this matter until my hon. friend brought it up to-night, but that is the information I have with respect to the case. I may add that surely the officials of the department ought to be the judges of whether or not a man is capable of filling a position after he is given a trial. If he had not received a trial it would be a different matter, but I am bound to say that I shall have to accept the opinion of my officials against any outside suggestions as to efficiency or anything else with respect to the department. I do not know anything about this case; it has been dealt with by the department officially, and the officials of the department must be the judges of a man's qualification to fill a position after he is given a fair and impartial trial.

Does the minister

The gravamen of this charge is that the department never intended that this man should retain the position. That would appear to be a clear case of fraud, and more than that there is the suggestion of political interference.

I should be very glad to give the minister all the information I have, and I would ask that he consider the holding of an investigation. Is it the policy of the department to lease Indian lands to orientals?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am informed that where they are available for leasehold, Indian lands are leased to orientals.

On page 1311 of Hansard of this year appears an answer by the minister to a question asked by the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer). A list is shown of about 32 orientals who have obtained leases on the Kamloops No. 1, Tsooahadie, "foreshore", Tsussie, Whonock and Musqueam reserves. I presume the minister knows of the agitation in British Columbia against the leasing of lands to orientals. He knows the foothold they are getting on lands in that province. I suggest to the minister that this is a policy the department should not pursue. Is there any particular reason why such a policy should be pursued?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I know of no particular reason. So far as I am aware, [DOT]the oriental rents property freely in British Columbia for the purpose of raising vegetables. The Indian department is not unique in the fact that it happens to have a few leases with orientals, who, so far as I know make very good gardeners; they take good care of the land and we get the rentals from them. There is no difficulty about getting our rentals. They are not receiving possession of the land in any way; it is merely on leasehold. I may say frankly, if Anglo-Saxons wish to rent the land they would certainly have the privilege, but I do not know that we should take the ground that we would absolutely refuse to lease lands to orientals unless that were a general policy in British Columbia and then, of course, we would acquiesce in it. The hon. member knows the oriental is a very large leaseholder in British Columbia.

The minister says that the orientals take good care of the land. Perhaps the minister does not know. As a matter of fact the orientals do just the opposite; they use up the land. It is estimated that if an oriental can have land for five years, its productive qualities are practically nil for quite a long period after. The minister has not that information, I presume.

My hon.
friend knows that right at his own home on the delta there is a very large settlement of orientals who have been there for a number of years. I happen to know that from observation. I had not heard they were leaving the land; they are farming it under leasehold. I had not heard that they were more extravagant in the use of land or took the life out of it more quickly than their white competitors. That is news to me, I confess.

Mr. MeQUARRIE: I want to ask another question in regard to unused Indian reserves. What is the policy of the government in connection with lands that are not being occupied by Indians at all? How many reserves have we like that in British Columbia?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I think we have in the neighbourhood of 1,200 in the province of British Columbia. I frankly confess we are not anxious to sell Indian lands, but when there are no Indians going to make use of them and they are of any particular value for agricultural purposes, they are usually sold or put under leasehold. Use is being made of them in some way, but the Indians of course receive the benefit of the receipts from the leases, and in this way we are assisted in carrying on the Indian work. As I say, we are not keen on selling Indian lands; we believe there is little enough land reserved for the Indians without depleting it further.
Mr. MeQUARRIE: When the department proceeds to lease lands, does it advertise them in any way or give opportunity to the public generally to know that such lands are for rental?

have applications for them and we seek to make known, in the locality in which the land is located, the fact that it is for rental. Perhaps the minister will give us a few words of explanation in connection with the item of $137,000 for the prevention of the spread of tuberculosis. I had a communication in respect to that the other day.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We are not anything like meeting the requirements of the case in regard to the suppression of tuberculosis amongst the Indians. Indeed, there is in Canada scarcely a band of Indian which is not more or less affected by tuberculosis.
Unfortunately the disease has spread to rather an alarming degree, so much so that we are really anxious about it. I am asking for the apointment of an assistant Indian medical officer, but even that does not touch the fringe of the question. Something further will have to be done, and a very considerable sum of money spent on this work in order to meet the situation'. I am having a survey made at the present time of the hospital facilities in every province in Canada, because we believe, rightly or wrongly, that it will be more economical for the department to work through the existing hospitals of the provinces than to attempt to set up large institutions of our own with the incidental cost. Of course in some instances we shall have to establish hospitals. Moreover, growing out of this is another demand, a demand for some sort of institution to house our old people, but I frankly confess our chief cause of alarm at the moment is tuberculosis and the ravages of this disease amongst the Indians and also the danger of the spreading into the communities that surround them as a result of so much of it being found on the reserves. Year by year we shall have to increase the vote for this purpose. I consider it a real menace and we are giving it very careful attention in the hope of meeting the situation as far as it is .posable to do so, not to eradicate,, but to suppress, if possible, the spread of the malady.

Last week I was at the
Byron hospital near London and I saw some Indian inmates of that hospital. During the past year I had occasion to observe the ravages of this disease in the Sarcee band near Calgary, where the band is certainly in a very precarious condition, where diseases of other kinds than tuberculosis have undermined the vitality of the survivors, and something must be done. The same thing is equally true in regard to other reserves in Alberta. I have had no opportnuity to see other reserves but one, and therefore I cannot with any degree of certainty speak about the matter. The minister anticipated a suggestion I was going to make to him, and it is this: We have a Department of Health and there should be the closest cooperation between the two departments. This overlapping is one of the things that disturb people greatly. The federal Department of Health should be of some service in matters of this kind. The hon. gentleman has referred to a subject that, I think, is of considerable importance, namely, the tying of the efforts of the department to those of the provincial organizations in some way. I do not know just how this can best
Supply-Indian Affairs

be accomplished. Take, for instance, the large institution near Robertson, west of Calgary, where large numbers of tubercular patients are being treated. From the inquiries I have made, it did not seem to me you could take the Indian patients to that sanatorium and have them treated with the other patients there..

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
What we
are doing-and we are trying to extend it- is to provide a sum of money to build extensions to those institutions, and they are operated as Indian annexes.

The hon. member knows what was done at Gleichen in connection with trying to put up little houses for them. It is their way of living that makes them so susceptible to the inroads of this disease. Certainly there are a great many people who are intensely concerned as to whether or not the existing conditions are not a menace to the public health of the surrounding community, as the minister has said. The deaths last year were very considerable, especially among the younger men and women on the reserves. The sum of $137,000 properly expended in one year in a concentrated effort at one particular point might provide facilities that would ensure that community against the ravages of this disease being so apparent next year, but a sum like $137,000 spread over as thinly as it has to be to take care of the whole situation, I am afraid, accomplishes very little good. I am bound to say that the facilities that have been provided in connection with the Sarcee and Blackfoot reserves and at one or two other places have done an amazing amount of good. But the Indian does not take kindly to the preventive measures that have to be taken to ensure anything like reasonable results. The reason I brought this matter up was that there might be on Hansard for the benefit of those who are tremendously interested in this matter a statement from the minister to which I could refer them, indicating a realization on his part of the dangers of the situation and as to what steps are being 'taken, not to eradicate, but to bring about an attitude of mind on .the pairt of those concerned by which they will 'let nature operate so as to prevent their becoming victims of tuberculosis.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
We have
been expending very large sums of money on the building of educational institutions, and I think we have now reached the stage where we shall not require so much money for that purpose. Both this year and last, in conjunction with the Department of Health at Ottawa and the provincial departments of

health, we have been making a survey with a view to establishing additions to the institutions already built to take care of the Indians who are suffering from this and other diseases.

May I suggest that there is this point to be remembered? The Indians are more susceptible to any disease taken from the white men than are the white men themselves, and a good deal of the work done should be directed not so much to taking care of the Indian after he has taken the disease as to preventing him from taking it. Tuberculosis is a disease which comes upon patients particularly after having had measles, and keeping the Indians from getting such diseases as measles will render them less susceptible to tuberculosis. Preventive measures of that sort will do more good than looking after the Indian after he has taken the disease.

force amounted to $627,595; patrol boats and provision for new boats, $922,317; patrol cars in operation, 120, valued at $139,600; travelling expenses, investigating and patrol officers, $123,000. Those items total $1,812,512. In British Columbia there are sixteen officers. In the western district, comprising Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba-I am afraid my hon. friend is not getting this information.
My hon. friend knows it is not the information I want. I have those figures before me.

I do not know what the
hon. gentleman wants. If he will wait a moment the chief of the preventive service will be here.

I will not bother the
minister now; he will not finish to-night anyway.
Is special consideration given to returned soldiers for appointment as preventive officers?

We observe the same principle, as far as possible, that we do in the income tax department.

I should like to
know why in my county all the preventive officers have been selected for the reason that they are dyed-in-the-wool supporters of this government. There is not a single preventive officer in my county who is a returned soldier, although there are many returned soldiers in the locality who would be eligible for the positions. Is a former rum seller eligible for a position in the preventive service?
Not if we know it.

The first man arrested for operating an illicit still in my county proved to the satisfaction of the court that he had purchased the still from the preventive officer who arrested him. The preventive service in Nova Scotia is nothing but a cheap political machine.

And in other parts of
the country as well.

The thing is an
absolute farce.
I merely say in reply, Mr. Chairman, that no appointment is made without the recommendation of the chief of the preventive service.

Where does he get his
recommendations?

The chief of the preventive
service is instructed never to recommend anybody who he is satisfied is not competent.

Take my own constituency of Inverness; upon whose recommendations did the minister make the appointments? No single appointment was made at the request of the chief of the preventive service; it was made at the request and upon the recommendation of the defeated Liberal candidate.

I merely have to repeat
that there has not been one appointment made except upon the recommendation of the chief of the preventive service.

Every appointment
in my constituency has been made upon the recommendation of the defeated Liberal candidate.
Perhaps I am wrong-

The minister is
wrong.

My hon. friend does not
even know what I am going to say. Probably I am wrong anyway, he thinks. I was
going to say that I doubt very much whether he himself made any recommendations to me with regard to any officer whom he desired appointed.
Why not?

Because it would
be of no use. The preventive service in Nova Scotia is a political machine. Every single appointment made in my county was made upon the recommendation of the defeated Liberal candidate, and I challenge the minister to contradict that statement.
I have already answered it.
I notice a vote to provide for the expense of maintenance of revenue cruisers, and so on, amounting to 81,812,000. It was $2,007,000 last year. How much of that vote has been spent?

The total expenditure last
year on the preventive service was $1,658,864.51. There was some liability on account of boats building which was carried over into the next year.

How many months
in the year are those preventive officers supposed to work?
Nearly all full time-twelve months in the year. The boat crews are not on full time.

Are they paid by
the month or by the year?

The land officers are all on
a yearly basis. The crews on the boats are on a monthly basis.

I know one man
in my county who has been home on his farm six months, and never did any work at all in that period as a preventive officer. If the minister's answer is correct, that man was paid for doing nothing. This shows what a fine political machine the preventive service is.

We have some part time
officers.

This is not a part
time officer.
I will make inquiries, and if any officer in his constituency spent six months on his farm when he was supposed to be working for the department, I can assure my hon. friend he will be fired.

I thank the minister, for he will lose a very good Grit worker.

me a little more definite information I shall be very glad to have it.

Could the minister
furnish a list of the appointments of officers, together with their addresses, made to these special services during the past year in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island? I think that could be done without much difficulty.
Of the land force only?

No, of this class of
officer that we made special provision for.

The
patronage crew.

the law calls for.
I want the return supplementing that, bringing it down to date.

My hon. friend wants a
.'eturn showing the appointments made from April 1, 1929, to April 1, 1930, for the maritime provinces?
Quite so.
Names and addresses?
That is all. I have a number of letters before me.
I am not sure that it will be possible to have the information when the house opens to-morrow.
Are they as numerous as that?
We would have to search several records to get the information.
Now, now-

My hon. friend is smiling, and I also have to smile. I must say that I do not know how long it will take to get the information he wishes, but I am perfectly willing to give him all the information he wishes to have. I cannot say whether it will take five minutes or an hour.

I am sure the hon. minister knows that no one expects him to do that. There have been a number of appointments made, however, in relation to which the hon. member for Inverness has spoken.
I have a number of letters before me which might or might not be wholly accurate.
Often they are not.

That is true; we cannot always understand what people 'write when prejudiced; sometimes the statements they 
make are not wholly accurate. On the other hand it should not be very difficult to prepare a list of those who have been appointed from April 1st, 1929, to April 1st, 1930, in the three maritime provinces, giving their names and addresses. Unless the signs fail, I am sure the information would be very interesting.
On what recommendations does the minister accept captains on patrol boats?
The same recommendations upon which land preventive officers are accepted ; we accept the recommendations of the chief of the preventive service.

From
whom are the recommendations generally received? From whom does the chief preventive officer get the recommendations?

The chief preventive officer makes inquiry through the Marine department and ' through the examiner of masteis and ma/tes of the naval service. We have a record of their past services and satisfy ourselves as to their qualifications and as to where they have been employed.
Has the department in every case a record of past services? And by the way, I may tell the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. McPhee) that I may go over and see him for a minute or two.
I invite my hon. friend to come over.
You are one of the type who would not stay, if I did go over.

Am I
to understand that the past histories of these men are known to the department? Does the minister mean to give me that information? I ask that question for a very definite reason.

So far as we know all the captains of the vessels are thoroughly reliable men; if we find they are not, they are dismissed. I may say that we have had to dismiss some of the men in the preventive service; it is very difficult to get reliable men, and we have had to let a good many of them out; probably we will have to do so in the future.

Reliable from a navigation or a political standpoint?

I know my hon. friend does not want an answer to that question.

The minister said he would dismiss certain men for doing certain things. I may tell him that I want to have one of the preventive officers dismissed before the election. I ask the minister if he will dismiss from the preventive service a man in connection with whom it can be proved that he has been engaged in the liquor traffic for years.
Hear, hear.
He is a preventive officer, and for years he has sold liquor in the province of Nova Scotia.
If my hon. friend can produce the proof, yes.
I can, and gladly.
Does the minister know of any officer of that sort in the maritime preventive service who is a Conservative?
There might be, but I am not sure.
But so far as the minister knows, there are none.
I do not know that there are any, to be quite frank about it.

Since the minister has made the statement that the record is known in connection with each of these men engaged in the maritime preventive service, would he be willing to give this house their histories, and would he tell the house how many of them during the last four years have been engaged in the rum running business?
Is my hon. friend asking that question seriously?
Yes. I am.

I am perfectly willing to be fair in the matter, and perhaps I can be more or less humorous in connection with it; but surely my hon. friend does not ask me to say that I know how many men in that service are engaged in the rum running business.

According to the minister these men were appointed 2419-176
on their records, and he has told us that their records are known to the department, and because of their records they have received appointments. In view of that statement I want to know exactly how many of these men were known to the government when they were appointed.
Not one.

You have not their
records, then?
I know of one man who was on board a rum runner, and he was placed in the preventive service, and refused to sign a document stating that he had not been aboard a rum runner.
I must take this opportunity to recommend that the Minister of National Revenue should appoint the two Siamese twins on the other side of the house to act as preventive officers.

In reply to the suggestion made by my hon. friend, I think it would be a good idea to have him appointed to the preventive service. With his outstanding qualifications, with the absolute intellectual abyss which does duty as his head, he would be quite in line with the calibre of the men the minister is appointing to do this work in the province of Nova Scotia.
